p.seg: The former ruler of Wú, Tàibó,
was a descendant of Hòujì.
Hòujì's mother,
a woman of the Tái clan named Jiāng Yuán,
was the principal wife of Emperor Kù.
Being young and not yet pregnant,
she went wandering in the wilderness,
saw a giant's footprint and observed it,
her heart feeling joyful,
delighting in its shape and form,
and thus stepped on it, treading upon it.
Her body stirred,
her mind feeling as if touched by a human presence.
Later she became pregnant,
and fearing the calamity of an illicit affair,
then performed sacrifices to seek guidance,
claiming she had no husband,
yet had trodden upon God's footprint,
and Heaven still commanded her to bear the child.
Jiāng Yuán, finding it strange, abandoned the child in a narrow alley,
but oxen and horses passing by diverted their path to avoid it.
She again abandoned it in a forest,
but it happened there were many woodcutters there.
She then placed it on ice in a marsh,
and flocks of birds covered it with their feathers.
Thus Hòujì did not die.
Jiāng Yuán considered him divine,
retrieved and raised him,
and when grown, he was therefore named Qì (Abandoned).
As a child, he enjoyed planting trees, grains, mulberries, hemps, and the five cereals,
assessing the suitability of the five types of soil,
whether green, red, yellow, or black,
on hills, near water, high or low,
for millet, panicled millet, glutinous millet, and non-glutinous millet,
as well as beans, wheat, and rice,
each finding its proper principle.
When Yáo encountered the great flood,
the people were adrift and scattered,
so they dwelled on high ground.
Yáo invited Qì
to teach the people to live in the mountains,
creating plots according to the land,
and excelling in the techniques of cultivation.
After more than three years,
travelers showed no signs of hunger or want.
Thereupon, Yáo appointed Qì as the Master of Agriculture,
enfeoffing him in Tái,
bestowing the title Hòujì,
with the clan name Jī.
Hòujì went to his state and became a feudal lord.
Upon his death,
his son Bù Zhú succeeded him.
Encountering the decline of the Xià dynasty,
he lost his office,
and fled among the Róng and Dí tribes.
His grandson was Gōng Liú.
Gōng Liú was benevolent and kind,
walking without treading on living grass,
and diverting his cart to avoid reeds.
Gōng Liú avoided Xià Jié among the Róng and Dí,
transforming their customs,
and the people were influenced by his governance.
Upon Gōng Liú's death,
his son Qìng Jié succeeded him.
After eight generations, there came Gǔ Gōng Dǎnfǔ.
He cultivated the works of Gōng Liú and Hòujì,
accumulating virtue and practicing righteousness,
and was admired by the Dí people.
The Xūnyù Róng attacked him,
and Gǔ Gōng served them with dogs, horses, cattle, and sheep,
yet they did not cease their attacks.
He served them with hides, silk, gold, jade, and precious treasures,
and still they did not cease their attacks.
Gǔ Gōng asked:
"What is it that you desire?"
They replied:
"We desire your land."
Gǔ Gōng said:
"A noble man does not harm those he nurtures for the sake of nurturing,
for that is how states perish.
To bring harm upon oneself for this,
is something I will not abide."
Gǔ Gōng then took his staff and left Bīn,
crossing over Mount Liáng to dwell in Qízhōu.
He said:
"What difference is there between that ruler and me?"
The people of Bīn, fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers, led one another,
carrying the old and guiding the young,
bearing their cauldrons and pots to follow Gǔ Gōng.
After three months of settlement,
city walls were completed,
in one year, a town was formed,
in two years, a capital was established,
and the people increased fivefold from the beginning.
Gǔ Gōng had three sons:
the eldest named Tàibó,
the second named Zhòng Yōng,
Yōng also known as Wú Zhòng,
and the youngest named Jì Lì.
Jì Lì married a woman of the Tài Rèn clan,
and they bore a son named Chāng.
Chāng had auspicious signs of sageliness,
and Gǔ Gōng, recognizing Chāng's sageliness,
wished to pass the state to him through Chāng.
He said:
"He who will rise to kingly enterprise,
must be Chāng."
He therefore changed his name to Jì Lì.
Tàibó and Zhòng Yōng, perceiving the intention,
said:
"Lì
means 'to go to'."
They knew Gǔ Gōng wished to pass the state to Chāng.
When Gǔ Gōng fell ill,
the two feigned a reason to gather herbs at Mount Héng.
They then went to the Jīng Mán tribes,
cut their hair and tattooed their bodies,
adopting the clothing of the barbarians,
to show they were unfit for use.
Upon Gǔ Gōng's death,
Tàibó and Zhòng Yōng returned.
After attending the funeral,
they went back to the Jīng Mán.
The people of the state treated them as rulers and served them,
and they named themselves Gōu Wú.
Someone from Wú asked:
"What is the meaning in the name Gōu Wú?"
Tàibó replied:
"I, as the eldest, should have remained in the state,
but I cut off my line of succession.
The one who deserves the enfeoffment
is Wú Zhòng.
Therefore, I name myself Gōu Wú;
is it not appropriate?"
The Jīng Mán, considering this righteous,
followed and joined him, over a thousand households,
together establishing him as Gōu Wú.
Within a few years,
the people became prosperous and wealthy.
Encountering the decline of the late Yīn dynasty,
the feudal lords and kings of the Central States frequently engaged in warfare.
Fearing it would reach the Jīng Mán,
Tàibó thus built a city,
with a wall three lǐ and two hundred bù in circumference,
and an outer wall over three hundred lǐ,
located at the northwestern corner,
named Gù Wú.
The people all farmed within it.
When Gǔ Gōng fell ill,
nearing death,
he ordered Jì Lì to yield the state to Tàibó,
but after three offers, Tàibó did not accept.
Hence it is said:
"Tàibó thrice declined the world."
Thereupon, Jì Lì assumed governance,
cultivating the enterprise of the former kings,
and upholding the way of benevolence and righteousness.
Upon Jì Lì's death,
his son Chāng succeeded him,
with the title Xībó.
He followed the methods of Gōng Liú and Gǔ Gōng,
devoting himself to caring for the elderly,
and the world turned to him.
Xībó brought about great peace,
and Bó Yí came from the seashore to join him.
Upon Xībó's death,
his heir, Fā, succeeded him,
entrusting Zhōu and Shào to attack Yīn.
When the world was pacified,
he then proclaimed himself king,
posthumously honoring Gǔ Gōng as Tài Wáng,
and posthumously enfeoffing Tàibó in Wú.
When Tàibó died,
he was buried at Méilǐ Píngxū.
Zhòng Yōng succeeded him,
and he was known as Wú Zhòng Yōng.
Upon Zhòng Yōng's death,
his son Jì Jiǎn succeeded,
Jiǎn's son Shū Dá,
Dá's son Zhōu Zhāng,
Zhāng's son Xióng,
Xióng's son Suì,
Suì's son Kē Xiāng,
Xiāng's son Qiáng Jiū Yí,
Yí's son Yú Qiáo Yí Wú,
Wú's son Kē Lú,
Lú's son Zhōu Yáo,
Yáo's son Qū Yǔ,
Yǔ's son Yí Wú,
Wú's son Qín Chǔ,
Chǔ's son Zhuān,
Zhuān's son Pō Gāo,
Gāo's son Gōu Bì succeeded.
At that time,
Jìn Xiàn Gōng destroyed the northern Yú of Zhōu,
and the Duke of Yú thereby initiated Jìn's attack on the Guó clan.
Bì's son was Qù Qí,
Qí's son Shòu Mèng succeeded,
and Wú grew increasingly strong.
proclaimed himself king.
From the era of Tàibó to the time of Shòumèng,
they occasionally held court assemblies with the Central States,
and the state thus became hegemonic.
In the first year of Shòumèng's reign,
he visited the Zhōu court,
went to Chǔ,
and observed the rituals and music of the various lords.
Duke Chéng of Lǔ met him at Zhōnglí,
where Shòumèng inquired deeply about the rituals and music of the Duke of Zhōu.
Duke Chéng fully presented the rituals and music of previous kings,
and consequently sang of the customs of the Three Dynasties.
Shòumèng said:
"I dwell among the barbarians,
where it is customary to wear hair in a mallet-shaped knot.
How could we possess such attire as this?"
He then sighed and departed, saying:
"Alas,
such are the rituals!"
In his second year,
Shēngōng Wūchén, a senior official who had fled from Chǔ, came to Wú.
He was appointed as a diplomat,
taught the Wú people archery and charioteering,
and guided them to attack Chǔ.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was enraged,
sent Zǐ Fǎn to command the army,
and defeated the Wú forces.
From then on, the two states became enemies.
Thus, Wú began to interact with the Central States,
and became a rival to the various lords.
In his fifth year,
they attacked Chǔ
and defeated Zǐ Fǎn.
In his sixteenth year,
King Gōng of Chǔ, resentful that Wú had attacked them under Wūchén's influence,
raised an army to attack Wú,
but turned back upon reaching Héngshān.
In his seventeenth year,
Shòumèng appointed Wūchén's son Húyōng as chancellor,
entrusting him with state affairs.
In his twenty-fifth year,
Shòumèng fell ill and was near death.
He had four sons:
the eldest, Zhūfán;
the second, Yúzhài;
the third, Yúmèi;
and the youngest, Jìzhá.
Jìzhá was virtuous,
and Shòumèng wished to establish him as heir.
Jìzhá declined, saying:
"The rituals have established precedents;
how can we abandon the rituals of former kings
to follow a father's personal preference?"
Shòumèng then instructed Zhūfán:
"I wish to pass the state to Zhá;
do not forget my words."
Zhūfán replied:
"King Tài of Zhōu recognized the sagacity of the Western Earl,
set aside the elder and established the younger,
and the kingly way flourished.
Now, if you wish to confer the state upon Zhá,
I would willingly farm in the wilderness."
The king said:
"In the past, Zhōu's practice of virtue extended throughout the realm;
now, in this small state of ours, in the land of the Jīng barbarians,
how could you accomplish the task of a Son of Heaven?
Moreover, if you do not forget your predecessor's words,
you must pass the state in order until it reaches Jìzhá."
Zhūfán said:
"How dare I not obey your command?"
After Shòumèng's death,
Zhūfán, as the eldest legitimate son, took charge of affairs
and governed the state.
In the first year of King Zhūfán of Wú,
after the mourning period had ended,
he yielded the throne to Jìzhá,
saying:
"Before the former king passed away,
he was often restless at dawn,
and when I observed his expression,
his thoughts were on Jìzhá.
Moreover, three times he mournfully commanded me, saying:
'I know of Prince Zhá's virtue.'
He wished to set aside the elder and establish the younger,
and repeatedly spoke of it.
Although he did so,
my heart had already consented.
Yet the former king could not bring himself to act on his personal wish,
and entrusted the state to me.
How dare I disobey his command?
Now, the state
is yours."
I wish to fulfill the former king's intention."
Jìzhá declined, saying:
"The eldest legitimate son should rule the state;
this is not the former king's personal whim,
but the institution of the ancestral temple and state altars.
How can it be changed?"
Zhūfán said:
"If it can benefit the state,
what does it matter about the former king's command?
King Tài changed the succession to Jìlì,
and the two uncles entered the land of the Jīng barbarians,
eventually establishing a state,
and the way of Zhōu was accomplished.
Our predecessors never ceased to speak of this,
and you are well acquainted with it."
Zhá again declined, saying:
"In the past, when the Duke of Cáo died,
the illegitimate son survived while the legitimate heir perished,
and the lords and people of Cáo acted against righteousness in establishing a ruler.
Zǐ Zāng heard of this,
and returned home reciting poetry.
The ruler of Cáo feared,
and intended to establish Zǐ Zāng.
Zǐ Zāng departed,
thus upholding the way of Cáo.
Though I lack talent,
I wish to follow Zǐ Zāng's righteousness.
I sincerely wish to withdraw."
The people of Wú insisted on establishing Jìzhá,
but he refused and went to farm in the wilderness,
so the people of Wú gave up.
Zhūfán became arrogant and willful,
disrespectful toward spirits and gods,
and looked to heaven seeking death.
As he was dying,
he commanded his brother Yúzhài:
"You must pass the state to Jìzhá."
He then enfeoffed Jìzhá at Yánlíng,
bestowing upon him the title "Lord Jì of Yánlíng."
In the twelfth year of Yúzhài's reign,
King Líng of Chǔ assembled the lords to attack Wú,
besieged Zhūfāng,
and executed Qìng Fēng.
Qìng Fēng had repeatedly spied for Wú against Yúzhài,
hence the attack by Jìn and Chǔ.
King Yúzhài of Wú angrily said:
"Qìng Fēng came to Wú in desperation,
and I enfeoffed him at Zhūfāng
to show that I do not resent capable men."
He immediately raised an army to attack Chǔ,
capturing two cities before withdrawing.
In his thirteenth year,
Chǔ, resentful that Wú had attacked them over Qìng Fēng,
held a grudge that did not abate,
and attacked Wú.
They reached Gānxī,
where Wú struck them,
and the Chǔ army fled in defeat.
In his seventeenth year,
Yúzhài died,
and Yúmèi succeeded him.
In the fourth year of his reign,
he died.
They wished to pass the throne to Jìzhá,
but Jìzhá declined
and fled,
saying:
"My refusal to accept the throne
is clear.
In the past, the former ruler commanded,
and I have already adhered to Zǐ Zāng's righteousness.
I purify my person and conduct,
look up to the lofty and tread the path of honor,
dwelling only in benevolence.
As for wealth and honor to me,
they are like the autumn wind passing by my ears."
He then fled back to Yánlíng.
The people of Wú established Yúmèi's son Zhōuyú,
who was titled King Liáo of Wú.
In his second year,
King Liáo sent Prince Guāng to attack Chǔ,
to avenge the previous execution of Qìng Fēng.
The Wú army was defeated and lost their boats.
Guāng, fearing reprisal,
abandoned them,
but later recovered the king's boats and returned.
Guāng plotted to assassinate King Liáo,
but had no one to conspire with.
Secretly seeking a worthy man,
he appointed a skilled physiognomist as a market official in Wú.
In the fifth year,
the exiled minister of Chǔ, Wǔ Zǐxū, came to Wú seeking refuge.
Wǔ Zǐxū
was a man of Chǔ,
named Yún.
Yún's father was Shē,
and his elder brother was Shàng.
Their ancestor was named Wǔ Jǔ,
who served King Zhuāng of Chǔ with forthright remonstrance.
When the king had been on the throne for three years,
he neglected state affairs,
indulged in wine,
and reveled in sensual pleasures,
holding a Qín beauty in his left arm,
and a Yuè maiden in his right,
sitting amidst bells and drums, he decreed:
"Whoever dares to remonstrate
shall die!"
Thereupon, Wǔ Jǔ came forward and admonished:
"There is a great bird
that has alighted in the court of Chǔ,
neither flying nor crying for three years.
What bird is this?"
King Zhuāng responded:
"This bird does not fly,
but when it does, it will soar to the heavens.
It does not cry,
but when it does, it will startle everyone."
Wǔ Jǔ said:
"If it neither flies nor cries,
it will become a target for archers.
Once the arrows are suddenly released,
how could it soar to the heavens and startle everyone?"
Thereupon, King Zhuāng cast aside his Qín and Yuè women,
ceased the music of bells and drums,
employed Sūn Shū'áo,
entrusting him with state affairs,
and thus became hegemon over the realm,
his might subduing the various lords.
After King Zhuāng's death,
King Líng ascended.
He built the Zhānghuá Tower,
and ascended it with his ministers.
The king said:
"The tower is magnificent!"
Wǔ Jǔ remarked:
"I have heard that a ruler considers being honored with virtue as beauty,
bringing peace to the people as joy,
heeding advice as wisdom,
and achieving far-reaching goals as clarity.
I have not heard that the height of earth and timber, the carving of intricate patterns, the clear tones of metal and stone, or the mournful sounds of strings and bamboo are considered beauty.
Formerly, King Zhuāng built the Bàojū Tower,
whose height did not exceed that needed to observe the state's aura,
and size was only sufficient to accommodate banquet vessels.
The timber did not hinder defense preparations,
the expenses did not burden the official treasury,
the people were not disrupted in their seasonal tasks,
and officials did not alter court routines.
Now, you have spent seven years building this tower,
causing resentment among the people,
exhausting financial resources,
ruining the year's harvest,
plaguing the populace,
arousing anger among the lords,
and drawing slander from ministers.
Is this what the former king promoted or what a ruler should consider beautiful?
I am truly ignorant,
and do not understand what is meant."
King Líng immediately halted construction and removed the decorations,
and did not visit the tower again.
From then on,
the Wǔ family served as loyal ministers to Chǔ for three generations.
King Píng of Chǔ had a crown prince named Jiàn.
King Píng appointed Wǔ Shē as the Grand Tutor to the crown prince,
and Fèi Wújí as the Junior Tutor.
King Píng sent Wújí to arrange a marriage for the crown prince with a woman from Qín.
The Qín woman was exceptionally beautiful,
and Wújí reported to King Píng:
"The Qín woman is peerless in the world;
Your Majesty should take her for yourself."
The king then took the Qín woman as his consort,
favoring and loving her,
and she bore him a son, Zhēn.
He then arranged for the crown prince to marry a woman from Qí instead.
Wújí thus left the crown prince's service to serve King Píng.
Deeply concerned that once King Píng died and the crown prince ascended,
he would be harmed,
he further slandered Crown Prince Jiàn.
Jiàn's mother, of the Cài clan, was out of favor,
so the king sent the crown prince to guard Chéngfù,
to prepare border defenses.
Soon after,
Wújí incessantly spoke of the crown prince's faults,
saying:
"Because of the Qín woman incident,
the crown prince cannot but harbor resentment;
I urge Your Majesty to be on guard.
The crown prince resides in Chéngfù commanding troops,
forming alliances with foreign lords,
and plans to enter the capital to rebel."
King Píng then summoned Wǔ Shē for interrogation.
Shē, aware of Wújí's slander,
admonished the king:
"How can Your Majesty, because of a slanderous petty official, estrange your own flesh and blood?"
Wújí, seizing an opportunity,
further said:
"If Your Majesty does not act now,
his plans will succeed,
and you will be captured."
King Píng was enraged,
imprisoned Wǔ Shē,
and sent Fènyáng, the Marshal of Chéngfù, to kill the crown prince.
Fènyáng sent someone ahead to warn the crown prince:
"Leave quickly!
Otherwise, you will be executed."
In the third month,
the crown prince fled to Sòng.
Wújí again told King Píng:
"Wǔ Shē has two sons,
both capable;
if not killed,
they will become a threat to Chǔ.
We can use their father as a hostage to summon them."
The king sent an envoy to tell Shē:
"If you can get your two sons to come, you live;
otherwise, you die."
Wǔ Shē said:
"I have two sons,
the elder named Shàng,
the younger named Xū.
Shàng is kind, gentle, benevolent, and trustworthy;
if he hears my summons,
he will come immediately.
Xū, in his youth, was fond of civil arts,
and in adulthood, skilled in military strategy;
capable of governing the state with civil arts,
and pacifying the realm with military prowess,
upholding principles and enduring hardship,
bearing disgrace and shame,
he does not contest even when wronged,
and can accomplish great deeds.
He is a man of foresight;
how could he be summoned?"
King Píng, thinking Wǔ Shē was praising his sons,
immediately dispatched an envoy with a four-horse carriage,
sealed boxes and official seals,
to summon Zǐshàng and Zǐxū under false pretenses.
The order stated:
"Congratulations to you both;
your father Shē, for his loyalty, trustworthiness, kindness, and benevolence,
has been released from hardship and spared.
King Píng, inwardly ashamed of imprisoning a loyal minister,
and outwardly embarrassed before the lords,
has instead appointed Shē as State Chancellor,
and enfeoffed you two as marquises.
Shàng is granted the title of Hóngdū Marquis,
and Xū as Gài Marquis.
Your estates are less than three hundred lǐ apart,
and Shē, long imprisoned,
has missed you both dearly,
so he sent me to present the seals."
Shàng said:
"My father imprisoned for three years,
my heart has been grieved,
I have eaten without tasting food,
suffered hunger and thirst,
grieving day and night,
fearing my father would not survive.
If only my father is spared,
how could I dare covet the seals?"
The envoy said:
"Your father imprisoned for three years,
the king has now graciously pardoned him,
and with nothing else to reward,
he enfeoffs you two as marquises.
A single word should suffice;
what more is there to say?"
Shàng then went in to tell Zǐxū:
"Father has been spared from death,
we two are to be marquises,
the envoy is at the gate,
with seals and titles prepared;
you should meet the envoy."
Zǐxū said:
"Brother, please sit calmly,
let me divine for you.
Today is the jiǎzǐ day,
the hour is sì,
the earthly branch injures the sun below,
the energies do not harmonize,
the ruler deceives his minister,
the father deceives his son.
If we go now, we will die;
what marquises are there to speak of?"
Shàng said:
"It is not that I covet the marquisate,
but I long to see our father!
Even one meeting to bid farewell,
though it means death, would be as if living."
Wǔ Zīxū said:
"Do not go yet;
Father will surely spare me.
Chǔ fears my valor,
and dares not kill me.
If you mistakenly go,
you will certainly die with no escape."
Wǔ Shàng said:
"The love between father and son,
affection springs from within,
hoping to meet by chance,
to achieve mutual relief."
Then Zǐxū sighed and said:
"To be executed together with father,
what clarity would that bring to the world?
If the enmity is not avenged,
the shame will grow greater daily.
You go from here,
I depart from here determined."
Shàng wept and said:
"If I live,
I'll be laughed at by the world,
growing old on this earth,
and where would I go!
Unable to take revenge,
I'd be completely useless.
You possess literary and martial talents,
brave in strategy and planning,
the vengeance for father and brother,
you can carry out.
If I should return,
it would be heaven's blessing.
If I sink into oblivion,
that too would please me."
Zǐxū said:
"Go then,
I leave without looking back.
Don't wait until disaster strikes,
for then regret would be too late!"
They parted in tears,
and he went with the envoy.
Chǔ captured Wǔ Zǐshàng,
seized and imprisoned him.
They again sent men to pursue and capture Zǐxū.
Zǐxū then strung his bow and grasped his arrows, leaving Chǔ.
Chǔ pursued him,
and he saw his wife,
who said:
"Zǐxū has fled,
gone three hundred lǐ away."
The pursuers caught up in a deserted wilderness,
Zǐxū then drew his bow and aimed arrows intending to harm the pursuers,
who prostrated themselves and fled.
Zǐxū said:
"Report to your King Píng,
if he wants his state not destroyed,
release my father and brother.
If not,
Chǔ will become ruins."
The envoy returned and reported to King Píng,
who heard this,
and immediately dispatched a large army to pursue Zǐxū.
They reached the river,
but lost track of him,
returning without capturing him.
Zǐxū traveled to the great river,
looking up to heaven and weeping as he walked through forests and marshes,
saying:
"The King of Chǔ is without principle,
he killed my father and brother,
I wish to rely on the various states to take revenge!"
Hearing that Crown Prince Jiàn was in Sòng,
Zǐxū decided to go there.
When Wǔ Shē first heard of Zǐxū's escape,
he said:
"The rulers and ministers of Chǔ will soon suffer the hardships of war!"
Shàng reached Chǔ to join his father,
and both were executed in the marketplace.
Wǔ Yún fled to Sòng,
and on the way met Shēn Bāoxū,
saying to him:
"The King of Chǔ killed my father and brother,
what should I do about it?"
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"Alas!
If I advise you to take revenge on Chǔ,
that would be disloyal.
If I advise you not to take revenge,
that would show no familial feeling.
You should go on your way,
I cannot say more."
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that for parents' enmity,
one cannot share the same sky and tread the same earth;
for brothers' enmity,
one cannot share the same region or border;
for friends' enmity,
one cannot share the same neighborhood or village.
Now I will repay Chǔ's crime,
to wash away the shame of my father and brother."
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"If you can destroy it,
I can preserve it.
If you can endanger it,
I can secure it."
Zǐxū then fled to Sòng.
Duke Yuán of Sòng was untrustworthy in governing the state,
and the people hated him.
The senior official Huá Shì plotted to kill Duke Yuán,
the people sided with Huá Shì,
and thus great chaos erupted.
Zǐxū then fled with Crown Prince Jiàn to Zhèng,
where the people of Zhèng treated them with great courtesy.
Crown Prince Jiàn then went to Jìn.
Duke Qǐng of Jìn said:
"Since the Crown Prince is in Zhèng,
and Zhèng trusts him,
if the Crown Prince can act as an insider and destroy Zhèng,
I will enfeoff Zhèng to the Crown Prince."
The Crown Prince returned to Zhèng,
but before the plan was accomplished,
he happened to want to act privately with his followers,
who knew of his plot,
and reported it to Zhèng.
Duke Dìng of Zhèng and Zǐchǎn executed Crown Prince Jiàn.
Jiàn had a son named Shèng,
and Wǔ Yún fled with Shèng to Wú.
Arriving at Zhāo Pass,
the border official wanted to arrest them.
Wǔ Yún then deceitfully said:
"The reason the authorities are searching for me,
is for beautiful pearls.
Now I have lost them,
and am going to retrieve them."
The border official thus let them go.
They traveled on with Shèng,
pursuers behind them,
narrowly escaping capture.
Reaching the river,
a fisherman in a boat was coming upstream from below.
Zǐxū called to him,
saying:
"Fisherman, ferry me across!"
After repeating this twice,
the fisherman wanted to ferry him.
Just then someone was watching nearby,
so he sang instead:
"The sun and moon shine bright while time slips away,
I'll meet you by the reedy shore."
Zǐxū then waited by the reedy shore.
The fisherman sang again:
"The sun has set, my heart grieves with sorrow,
the moon has raced, why not cross now?
Matters grow urgent, what should be done?"
Zǐxū entered the boat,
the fisherman understood his intention,
and ferried him across to a distant shore.
After Zǐxū had crossed,
the fisherman looked at him,
noting his hungry appearance.
He then said:
"Wait for me under this tree,
I'll fetch food for you."
After the fisherman left,
Zǐxū grew suspicious,
and hid himself in the deep reeds.
After a while,
the fisherman returned,
bringing wheat meal, preserved fish soup, and jar liquor.
Searching under the tree,
he didn't find him,
so he sang while calling out:
"Man in the reeds,
man in the reeds,
are you not a man in distress?"
After repeating this twice,
Zǐxū emerged from the reeds and responded.
The fisherman said:
"I saw you looked hungry,
and fetched food for you,
why do you suspect me?"
Zǐxū said:
"My life belongs to Heaven,
now it belongs to you, elder,
how dare I suspect you?"
After the two finished eating and drinking,
as they were about to leave,
Zǐxū took off his hundred-gold valued sword and gave it to the fisherman:
"This is my former lord's sword,
with seven stars in it,
worth a hundred in gold,
I give this in return."
The fisherman said:
"I have heard of Chǔ's decree:
whoever captures Wǔ Zǐxū,
will be rewarded with fifty thousand dàn of grain,
and the nobility of Zhíguī.
Why would I covet a hundred-gold sword?"
He thus declined and would not accept it,
saying to Zǐxū:
"You must leave quickly,
do not linger,
or you will be captured by the Chu."
Zǐxū said:
"May I ask the elder's name?"
The fisherman replied:
"Today is perilous,
two outlaws have met;
I am what you call the ferryman of the Chu outlaw.
When two outlaws encounter each other,
their identities are understood in silence—
what use is there for a name?
You are the man among the reeds,
I am the old fisherman;
if you achieve wealth and honor, do not forget me."
Zǐxū said:
"I promise."
After he left,
he cautioned the fisherman:
"Cover your jar of provisions,
do not let it be exposed."
The fisherman agreed.
Zǐxū had taken a few steps
when he looked back at the fisherman,
who had already capsized his boat and drowned himself in the river.
Zǐxū fell silent.
He then journeyed to Wú,
fell ill on the way,
and begged for food in Lìyáng.
By chance, he encountered a woman pounding silk by the Lài River,
with rice in her basket.
Zǐxū approached her
and said:
"Madam,
may I have a meal?"
The woman replied:
"I live alone with my mother,
thirty and unmarried;
I cannot give you food."
Zǐxū said:
"Madam, aiding a desperate man with a little food—
what suspicion could there be?"
The woman realized he was no ordinary man
and thus consented.
She opened her basket,
served him the rice and broth,
and knelt to offer it.
Zǐxū ate only twice and stopped.
The woman said:
"You have a long journey ahead,
why not eat your fill?"
After Zǐxū had eaten and was leaving,
he said to the woman:
"Cover your pot of broth,
do not let it be exposed."
The woman sighed:
"Alas!
I have lived alone with my mother for thirty years,
preserving my chastity and integrity,
unwilling to marry;
how could it be proper to feed a man,
transgressing etiquette?
I cannot bear this.
Go on your way."
As Zǐxū left,
he glanced back at the woman,
who had already thrown herself into the Lài River.
Oh!
How chaste, bright, and steadfast—
truly a woman of manly virtue!
When Zǐxū reached Wú,
he let his hair loose and feigned madness,
went barefoot with a mud-smeared face,
and begged in the market.
The market-goers watched,
but none recognized him.
The next day,
a Wú market official skilled in physiognomy saw him
and said:
"I have judged many men's faces,
but never seen one like this.
Is he not a fugitive minister from a foreign state?"
He then reported to King Liáo of Wú,
describing the man's appearance in detail:
"Your Majesty should summon him."
King Liáo said:
"Bring him in with you."
Prince Guāng heard of this
and secretly rejoiced:
"I heard that Chǔ executed the loyal minister Wǔ Shē,
and his son Zǐxū,
brave and wise,
must be seeking to avenge his father,
and has come to Wú."
He intended to secretly nurture him.
The market official then entered with Zǐxū to see the king;
King Liáo marveled at his imposing stature:
ten feet tall,
with a waist ten arm-spans around,
and a foot between his eyebrows.
King Liáo conversed with him for three days,
and his words never repeated.
The king said:
"He is a worthy man."
Zǐxū, knowing the king favored him,
each time he entered to speak,
exuded a valiant spirit,
gradually mentioning his vengeance,
with a look of deep anguish.
King Liáo understood
and wanted to raise an army to avenge him.
Prince Guāng plotted to assassinate King Liáo,
fearing Zǐxū's closeness to the king would thwart his plan,
so he slandered:
"Wǔ Xū's advice to attack Chǔ
is not for Wú's sake,
but only to avenge his personal grudge;
Your Majesty should not use him."
Zǐxū knew Prince Guāng intended to harm King Liáo,
and said:
"That Guāng has ambitions within;
one cannot discuss external affairs with him."
He went to see King Liáo
and said:
"I have heard that feudal lords do not raise armies for a common man against another state."
King Liáo asked:
"Why do you say that?"
Zǐxū replied:
"Feudal lords govern with authority,
not acting on impulse to rescue emergencies with armies;
now Your Majesty rules the state with power,
raising troops for a common man—
it is not righteous.
I dare not follow Your Majesty's command."
The King of Wú then desisted.
Zǐxū withdrew to farm in the countryside,
seeking a brave man to recommend to Prince Guāng,
hoping to gain his favor.
He found the brave man Zhuān Zhū.
Zhuān Zhū
was from Tángyì.
When Wǔ Xū fled Chǔ for Wú,
he met him on the road.
Zhuān Zhū was engaged in a fight,
about to confront his enemy,
his fury like that of ten thousand men,
overwhelmingly fierce,
yet one call from his wife made him turn back.
Zǐxū, surprised, asked him:
"Why does your rage run so deep,
yet you retreat at a woman's voice—
is there a reason?"
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Look at my demeanor—
do I seem a fool?
Why such a crude question?
To bow beneath one man
ensures rising above ten thousand."
Zǐxū then observed his features:
prominent forehead and deep-set eyes,
tiger's chest and bear's back,
fierce yet capable of endurance,
and knew he was a warrior;
he secretly befriended him,
intending to use him.
When Prince Guāng sought conspirators,
he introduced him to Prince Guāng.
Guāng, having obtained Zhuān Zhū, treated him with respect.
Prince Guāng said:
"Heaven has sent you, sir, to aid my rootless self."
Zhuān Zhū asked:
"When former King Yúmò died,
Liáo ascended—
it was his rightful share.
Why does the prince wish to harm him?"
Guāng replied:
"Former Lord Shòumèng had four sons:
the eldest, Zhūfán,
was my father;
next was Yúzhài,
then Yúmò,
and the youngest was Jìzhá,
the most worthy.
As he was dying,
he decreed succession by the eldest,
passing to Jìzhá.
But Jìzhá was on a mission,
absent in another state and not returned.
When Yúmò died,
the state was vacant,
and the one to stand should have been the eldest's line.
The eldest's heir
is myself.
How then should Liáo rightfully succeed?
My strength is weak, unaided in affairs of state;
without employing men of might,
how can I secure my ambition?
Even if I succeed,
when Jìzǐ returns from the east,
he will not depose me."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Why not have a close minister speak casually by the king's side,
relaying the former king's decree,
to subtly convey the intention,
letting him know where the state rightfully belongs?
Why must you privately prepare swordsmen,
thereby discarding the late king's virtue?"
Guāng said:
"Liáo is inherently greedy and relies on force,
knowing only the benefits of advancement,
blind to retreat and concession.
Thus I seek men who share my concerns,
wishing to join forces with them,
only you, master, can interpret this meaning."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Your words are quite explicit,
what do you intend for the prince?"
Guāng said:
"Not so.
These are words concerning the state,
a humble man cannot carry them out,
I can only entrust my fate."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"I await the prince's command."
Prince Guāng said:
"The time is not yet right."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Whenever one wishes to kill a ruler,
one must first learn what he delights in.
What does the King of Wú delight in?"
Guāng said:
"He delights in fine flavors."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Which flavor pleases him most?"
Guāng said:
"He is especially fond of roasted fish."
Zhuān Zhū then left,
and went to Lake Tài to learn how to roast fish.
After three months he had mastered the flavor,
and sat quietly awaiting Prince Guāng's command.
In the eighth year,
Liáo sent the prince to attack Chǔ,
where he greatly defeated the Chǔ army,
and thereupon welcomed the mother of the former crown prince Jiàn from Zhèng.
The lord of Zhèng presented Jiàn's mother with pearl and jade hairpins and earrings,
wishing to atone for the fault of killing Jiàn.
In the ninth year,
Wú sent Guāng to attack Chǔ,
capturing Jūcháo and Zhōnglí.
The reason Wú attacked them was that initially,
a woman from the border town of Píliáng in Chǔ,
and a maiden raising silkworms from a Wú border town,
quarreled over mulberry trees on the boundary.
The two households attacked each other,
the Wú side did not prevail,
so they escalated to mutual attacks,
wiping out Wú's border town.
Wú was enraged,
thus they attacked Chǔ and took two towns before leaving.
In the winter of the twelfth year,
King Píng of Chǔ died.
Wǔ Zǐxū said to Báigōng Shèng:
"King Píng has died,
my ambition remains unfulfilled.
Yet as long as Chǔ state exists,
what have I to worry about?"
Báigōng remained silent and did not reply,
while Wǔ Zǐxū sat weeping in his chamber.
In the thirteenth year,
spring,
Wú wished to take advantage of Chǔ's funeral to attack them.
They sent princes Gàiyú and Zhúyōng with troops to besiege Chǔ,
and sent Jì Zhá to Jìn,
to observe the movements of the various states.
Chǔ dispatched troops to cut off the Wú army's retreat,
so the Wú troops could not return.
At this, Prince Guāng's mind became agitated.
Wǔ Xū, knowing Guāng recognized the opportunity,
then advised Guāng saying:
"Now the King of Wú is attacking Chǔ,
his two brothers are leading the troops,
their fortune is unknown.
The matter of Zhuān Zhū,
is now urgent.
The moment will not come again,
it must not be lost."
Thereupon the prince visited Zhuān Zhū and said:
"Now my two brothers are attacking Chǔ,
and Jìzǐ has not yet returned.
At this very moment,
if we do not seek, what shall we gain?
The time must not be lost,
moreover, I am the true royal heir."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"Liáo can be killed.
His mother is old,
his sons are young,
his brothers are attacking Chǔ,
and Chǔ has cut off their retreat,
now Wú is externally besieged by Chǔ,
and internally empty of staunch ministers,
thus he can do nothing to us."
In the fourth month,
Prince Guāng concealed armored soldiers in a cellar room,
prepared a feast, and invited King Liáo.
Liáo said to his mother:
"Prince Guāng has prepared wine and invited me,
is there no risk of变故?"
His mother said:
"Guāng's heart is discontent,
he often has a look of shame and resentment,
you must be cautious."
King Liáo then donned three layers of táng iron armor,
had soldiers line the roads,
from the palace gate all the way to Guāng's door,
by the steps and mats on both sides were all Liáo's close relatives,
with seated and standing attendants all holding long halberds crossed.
When the wine was at its height,
Prince Guāng feigned foot ailment,
entered the cellar room to wrap his foot,
and had Zhuān Zhū place the Yúcháng dagger in the roasted fish and present it.
When he reached before King Liáo,
Zhuān Zhū then tore open the roasted fish,
and pushed forth the dagger,
the standing halberds crossed and pressed against Zhuān Zhū's chest,
his chest was severed and breast split open,
yet the dagger proceeded as before,
stabbing King Liáo,
piercing through his armor and out his back.
Once King Liáo was dead,
the attendants together killed Zhuān Zhū.
The guards were thrown into turmoil,
Prince Guāng released his armored soldiers,
to attack Liáo's followers,
and annihilated them all.
Thereupon he established himself,
becoming King HéLǘ of Wú.
He then enfeoffed Zhuān Zhū's son,
appointing him as a guest minister.
When Jì Zhá's mission ended and he returned,
arriving in Wú,
HéLǘ offered him the throne.
Jì Zhá said:
"If the former ruler's sacrifices are not abandoned,
the people are not without a lord,
the altars of soil and grain are served,
the state is not overturned,
then he is my ruler,
whom should I resent?
I mourn the dead and await the living,
biding heaven's will.
It was not I who caused the disorder,
I follow the one established,
such was the way of our predecessors."
He ordered mourning at Liáo's tomb,
then returned to his post and awaited orders.
The two princes Gàiyú and Zhúyōng, who were leading troops and trapped in the siege by Chǔ,
heard that Prince Guāng had killed King Liáo and made himself king,
so they led their troops and surrendered to Chǔ,
and Chǔ enfeoffed them in Shū.
In the first year of Hé Lǘ's reign,
he began appointing the virtuous and employing the capable,
dispensing kindness and practicing benevolence,
earning renown among the feudal lords for his righteousness.
Before his benevolence was fully extended,
and his kindness not yet implemented,
he feared his people would not submit,
and the feudal lords would not trust him.
Thus, he elevated Wǔ Zǐxū to the position of envoy,
treating him with the courtesy due a guest,
and consulted him on state affairs.
Hé Lǘ said to Zǐxū:
"I wish to strengthen the state and become a hegemon king;
how can this be achieved?"
Wǔ Zǐxū approached on his knees,
shedding tears and kowtowing as he said:
"Your servant
is a fugitive from the state of Chǔ,
abandoned by father and brothers,
my bones left unburied,
my spirit deprived of sacrificial offerings,
bearing guilt and enduring disgrace,
I came to pledge my life to Your Majesty,
fortunate not to be executed;
how dare I involve myself in governance?"
Hé Lǘ replied:
"If not for you, sir,
I would not have escaped being a captive envoy.
Now, fortunate to receive your guidance,
I have reached this point;
why hesitate midway?"
Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that a minister who offers counsel
should not remain in a perilous position;
yet once worries are dispelled and matters settled,
he will inevitably fall out of the ruler's favor."
Hé Lǘ said:
"Not so.
Without you, I have no one to fully consult;
why decline?
Our state is remote and isolated,
situated in the southeastern region,
with treacherous terrain and damp climate,
further plagued by river and sea hazards.
The ruler lacks defenses,
the people have nothing to rely on,
granaries are unbuilt,
fields lie uncultivated;
what should be done about this?"
After a long pause, Zǐxū responded:
"I have heard that the way to govern a state,
to secure the ruler and manage the people,
is the highest priority."
Hé Lǘ asked:
"How does one secure the ruler and govern the people?"
Zǐxū said:
"To secure the ruler, govern the people, establish hegemony, achieve kingship, and control distant lands from nearby,
one must first build city walls,
establish defenses,
fill granaries,
and maintain armories;
these are the methods."
Hé Lǘ said:
"Excellent.
Building city walls,
erecting granaries,
adapting to the terrain,
is there a way to harness the forces of heaven
to intimidate neighboring states?"
Zǐxū said:
"There is."
Hé Lǘ declared:
"I entrust the planning to you."
Zǐxū then had surveyors examine the land and taste the water,
modeling heaven and emulating earth,
to construct a great city.
Its circumference measured forty-seven lǐ.
It had eight land gates,
symbolizing the eight winds of heaven.
Eight water gates,
reflecting the eight directions of earth.
A smaller city was built,
ten lǐ in circumference,
with three hill gates.
The east side was left unopened
to cut off the influence of Yuè.
The Chāngmén was erected
to resemble the heavenly gate,
channeling the Chānghé wind.
The Shémén was established
to symbolize the earthly door.
Hé Lǘ intended to conquer Chǔ to the west,
which lay in the northwest,
so he built the Chāngmén to connect with heavenly energy,
renaming it the 'Breach Chǔ Gate.'
Aiming to annex Great Yuè to the east,
with Yuè in the southeast,
he erected the Shémén to subdue the rival state.
Wú corresponded to the celestial sign of Chén,
represented by the dragon,
so the small city's south gate featured upturned fins like two young dragons,
symbolizing dragon horns.
Yuè aligned with the Sì position,
embodied by the snake,
hence a wooden snake was placed on the south main gate,
facing inward to the north,
indicating Yuè's subordination to Wú.
With the city walls completed
and granaries equipped,
Hé Lǘ again tasked Zǐxū, Qū Gàiyú, and Zhú Yōng with mastering tactics, cavalry, archery, and charioteering,
though these skills had not yet been applied.
He commissioned Gānjiàng to forge two famous swords.
Gānjiàng was a man of Wú,
who studied under the same master as Ōuyězǐ,
both skilled in sword-making.
Yuè had previously presented three swords,
which Hé Lǘ treasured upon receiving,
prompting him to order the swordsmith to create two more:
one named Gānjiàng,
the other Mòyé.
Mòyé was Gānjiàng's wife.
To make the swords,
Gānjiàng gathered the finest iron from five mountains
and the most excellent metal from all directions.
He awaited celestial and terrestrial signs,
with yin and yang shining together,
deities overseeing the process,
and heavenly energies descending,
yet the essence of the metal would not melt and flow.
Perplexed, Gānjiàng could not determine the cause.
Mòyé asked:
"You are renowned to the king for your skill in sword-making;
he tasked you with forging a sword,
but three months have passed without success;
is there a reason?"
Gānjiàng replied:
"I do not understand the principle."
Mòyé said:
"The transformation of divine objects
requires human sacrifice to complete.
Now, in your sword-making,
could it be that it awaits the right person to succeed?"
Gānjiàng said:
"When my master smelted,
the metal refused to melt,
so both he and his wife entered the furnace,
and only then was the object completed.
To this day, later generations,
when smelting at the mountain,
don hemp mourning clothes and headbands,
before daring to cast metal there.
Now, my sword refuses to transform;
could it be for the same reason?"
Mòyé said:
"If the master knew that scorching his body would complete the object,
why should I find it difficult?"
Thereupon, Gānjiàng's wife cut off her hair and trimmed her nails,
casting them into the furnace.
She had three hundred boys and girls bellows the blast and load charcoal,
whereupon the metal melted,
and the swords were thus forged.
The male was named Gānjiàng,
the female Mòyé.
The male bore tortoise-shell patterns,
the female had diffuse grain.
Gānjiàng hid the male sword,
presenting only the female to Hé Lǘ,
who valued it greatly.
After obtaining the treasured sword,
it happened that the Lǔ envoy Jìsūn was visiting Wú on a mission.
Hé Lǘ ordered his sword officer to present Mòyé to him.
Jìsūn noticed a notch on the blade as large as a millet grain
and sighed:
"How magnificent!
This sword.
Even the finest masters of superior states
could not surpass this!
When a sword is perfected,
Wú will achieve hegemony.
If it is flawed,
then it will perish.
Though I admire it,
how can I accept it!"
He declined and left.
Hé Lǘ, cherishing Mòyé,
also ordered the production of metal hooks throughout the state,
proclaiming:
"Whoever can make an excellent hook
will be rewarded with a hundred pieces of gold."
Many in Wú crafted hooks,
and one among them, coveting the king's generous reward,
killed his two sons,
using their blood to temper the metal,
thus forging two hooks.
He presented them to Hé Lǘ,
arriving at the palace gate to seek his reward.
The king said:
"Many are the makers of hooks,
yet you alone seek reward.
How does your hook differ from those of the other masters?"
The hook maker replied:
"When I made the hooks,
in my greed I killed my two sons,
and smeared their blood to complete two hooks."
The king then displayed all the hooks to him:
"Which ones are they?"
The king had many hooks,
similar in shape and form,
and couldn't identify them.
Thereupon, the hook master faced the hooks and called his two sons' names:
"Wú Hóng, Hù Jī,
I am here.
The king doesn't know your divine power."
As his voice faded,
two hooks flew forth together,
and attached to their father's chest.
The king of Wú was greatly astonished,
and said:
"Alas!
I have truly wronged you."
He then rewarded him with a hundred pieces of gold,
and henceforth wore the hooks constantly on his person.
In the sixth month,
when he intended to raise an army,
Bái Xǐ of Chǔ happened to come seeking refuge.
The king of Wú asked Zǐxū:
"What kind of man is Bái Xǐ?"
Zǐxū said:
"Bái Xǐ is
the grandson of Bái Zhōulí of Chǔ.
Píng Wáng executed Zhōulí,
so Xǐ fled,
and hearing that I was in Wú, he has come."
Hélǘ said:
"What crime did Zhōulí commit?"
Zǐxū said:
"Bái Zhōulí,
the Left Assistant of Chǔ,
also known as Xì Wǎn,
served Píng Wáng.
Píng Wáng favored him,
often conversing with him all day,
and dining together from morning.
Fèi Wújì saw this and grew jealous,
so he told Píng Wáng:
'Your Majesty's affection for Wǎn
is known throughout the state.
Why not prepare a feast,
and visit Wǎn's home,
to show the ministers how much you value Wǎn?'
Píng Wáng said:
'Good.'
So a banquet was arranged at Xì Wǎn's residence.
Wújì advised Wǎn:
'Píng Wáng is very resolute and fond of military affairs,
you must deliberately display arms in the hall and courtyard.'
Wǎn believed his words,
and acted accordingly.
When Píng Wáng arrived, he was greatly startled and said:
'What is Wǎn up to?'
Wújì said:
'He likely harbors treasonous intentions to assassinate.
Your Majesty should leave quickly,
the situation is unpredictable.'
Píng Wáng was enraged,
and had Xì Wǎn executed.
The feudal lords heard of this,
and none did not sigh in regret.
Xǐ, hearing that I was in Wú,
thus came here,
and requests an audience."
Hélǘ met Bái Xǐ and asked him:
"My state is remote and isolated,
bordering the eastern sea,
yet I have heard of how your ancestor suffered from Chǔ Jīng's fierce wrath,
and Fèi Wújì's slanderous tongue.
You have not considered our state too far to come;
what instruction do you have for me?"
Xǐ said:
"I am a fugitive from Chǔ's injustice,
my ancestor was guiltless,
yet wrongly suffered violent execution.
I heard that Your Majesty had taken in Wǔ Zǐxū in his distress,
so I have traveled a thousand lǐ without regard for the distance,
to come and submit to you,
only begging that Your Majesty grant me death if need be."
Hélǘ pitied him,
appointed him as a senior official,
and consulted him on state affairs.
The Wú official Bèi Lí, during a banquet,
asked Zǐxū:
"Why do you trust Xǐ upon meeting him?"
Zǐxū said:
"My grievance is the same as Xǐ's.
Have you not heard the song by the river?
Those with the same ailment pity each other,
those with the same sorrow aid one another.
Startled birds in flight
gather together.
Waters from the rapids
flow on reunited.
The northern horse stands facing the north wind,
the Yuè swallow basks in the sunlight.
Who does not cherish what is close to them,
and grieve for what they long for?"
Bèi Lí said:
"Your words speak of external matters,
but is there an inner meaning to resolve doubts?"
Zǐxū said:
"I do not see it."
Bèi Lí said:
"I observe Xǐ's character:
he has the gaze of a hawk and the walk of a tiger,
a nature bent on usurping merit and arbitrary killing;
he cannot be trusted."
Zǐxū did not agree with his words,
and together they served the king of Wú.
In the second year,
King Hé Lǘ of Wú, having previously assassinated King Liáo,
was troubled by Qìng Jì's presence in a neighboring state,
fearing he would ally with other lords to attack Wú.
He asked Wǔ Zǐ Xū:
"In the past, Zhuān Zhū served me with great loyalty.
Now I hear Prince Qìng Jì is conspiring with the feudal lords,
I cannot savor my food,
nor rest peacefully in my bed,
and entrust this matter to you."
Wǔ Zǐ Xū replied:
"Your servant lacks loyalty and virtue,
having already plotted against King Liáo with you in private chambers.
Now to again seek harm against his son,
I fear this goes against Heaven's will."
Hé Lǘ said:
"When King Wǔ of Zhōu defeated Zhòu and later killed Wǔ Gēng,
the people of Zhōu bore no resentment.
If we follow such precedent,
how could it offend Heaven!"
Wǔ Zǐ Xū said:
"I serve my king,
seeking to complete Wú's sovereignty,
so why should I fear?
The man I know well
is of humble origins,
but willing to join the plot."
The King of Wú said:
"My concern is
this enemy possesses the strength of ten thousand men;
how could a humble man succeed in plotting against him?"
Wǔ Zǐ Xū said:
"Though this humble man plots affairs,
he has the effectiveness of ten thousand men's strength."
The king said:
"Who is he?
Tell me his name."
Wǔ Zǐ Xū said:
"His surname is Yāo,
his name Lí.
I once saw him humiliate the warrior Qiū Qiū Xū."
The king asked:
"How did he humiliate him?"
Wǔ Zǐ Xū said:
"Qiū Qiū Xū
was a man from the Eastern Sea,
sent as an envoy from Qí to Wú.
Passing by Huái River crossing,
he wanted to water his horse there.
The ferry officer said:
'There is a river god in the water,
who emerges at the sight of horses
to harm them.
Do not water your horse here.'
Xū said:
'What god would dare oppose
a warrior's duty?'
He ordered his attendant to water the horse,
and the river god indeed took his horse,
which sank.
Qiū Qiū Xū grew furious,
bared his upper body, drew his sword,
and entered the water to battle the god.
After days he emerged,
having lost an eye.
He then came to Wú,
attending a friend's funeral.
Relying on his bravery in battling the water god,
he acted arrogantly toward the officials at the funeral,
speaking rudely
with an overbearing manner.
Yāo Lí sat opposite him,
and all present couldn't bear his excessive pride in his strength.
Then Yāo Lí rebuked Xū:
'I've heard that when true warriors fight,
they don't shift their stance against the sun,
don't retreat a step against gods or ghosts,
and don't need shouts against men,
going forth alive or returning dead,
never accepting humiliation.
Now you fought a god in water,
lost your horse and control,
suffered the loss of an eye,
disfigured yet claiming bravery—
this shames true warriors.
Instead of dying by your enemy,
you cling to life,
yet still act arrogantly toward me!'
Thereupon,
Qiū Qiū Xū, cornered by this reproach,
burst with rage and resentment,
and planned to attack Yāo Lí that night.
Meanwhile,
Yāo Lí returned home after the banquet
and warned his wife:
'I humiliated warrior Qiū Qiū Xū at the grand funeral,
leaving him seething with anger.
He will surely come tonight—
be sure not to lock our door.'
That night,
Qiū Qiū Xū indeed went,
finding the door unlocked.
He entered the hall,
unbarred.
Went into the chamber,
unguarded.
Yāo Lí lay with hair loose, fearless.
Xū then gripped his sword, seized Yāo Lí and said:
'You have three faults deserving death—
do you know them?'
Lí said:
'No.'
Xū said:
'You shamed me before the crowd—
first death fault.
Returning home without locking doors—
second death fault.
Sleeping unguarded—
third death fault.
With three death faults,
you can't complain if killed.'
Yāo Lí said:
'I have no three death faults,
but you have three disgraces—
do you know them?'
Xū said:
'No.'
Yāo Lí said:
'I insulted you before thousands,
yet you didn't dare respond—
first disgrace.
Entering without coughing,
ascending silently—
second disgrace.
Drawing your sword first,
grabbing my head,
then daring to boast—
third disgrace.
With three disgraces yet threatening me—
isn't that shameful?'
Thereupon,
Qiū Qiū Xū threw down his sword and sighed:
'My bravery
was unchallenged by any,
but Lí surpasses me—
he is truly a warrior of the world.'
Having witnessed Yāo Lí thus,
I truly know his worth."
The King of Wú said:
"I wish to receive him at a banquet."
Wǔ Zǐ Xū then visited Yāo Lí, saying:
"The King of Wú has heard of your high principles,
and wishes you to meet him once."
So he went with Wǔ Zǐ Xū to see the King of Wú.
The king asked:
"What brings you here?"
Yāo Lí said:
"Your servant
comes from a thousand lǐ east of the capital.
I am small and weak,
stiffening in the wind,
prostrating before storms.
But if the king commands,
how dare I not exert full effort?"
The King of Wú doubted Wǔ Zǐ Xū recommending such a man,
and after a long pause,
remained silent.
Yāo Lí then stepped forward:
"Does the king worry about Qìng Jì?
I can kill him."
The king said:
"Qìng Jì's bravery
is renowned worldwide.
His sinews and bones are fiercely strong,
none among ten thousand can match him.
He outruns galloping beasts,
catches flying birds with his hands,
leaps and dashes with agility,
covering hundreds of lǐ effortlessly.
I once pursued him to the river,
four horses at full gallop couldn't catch up.
Shooting at him,
he dodged arrows in darkness, never hit.
Now your strength is no match."
Yāo Lí said:
"If the king intends it,
I can kill him."
The king said:
"Qìng Jì is wise and perceptive;
though stranded among the lords,
he doesn't submit to their officers."
Yāo Lí said:
"I've heard that to enjoy the comfort of wife and children
while neglecting duty to the king
is not loyalty.
To cherish family love
yet not remove the king's trouble
is not righteousness.
I will pretend to flee bearing false guilt,"
I beseech the king to execute my wife and children,
and sever my right hand,
so that Qìng Jì will surely trust me."
The king said:
"Agreed."
Yāo Lí then feigned offense and fled into exile,
whereupon the king of Wú seized his wife and children,
and had them burned and discarded in the marketplace.
Yāo Lí then fled to the various states spreading grievances,
making his innocence known throughout the world.
Subsequently, he went to Wèi,
seeking an audience with Qìng Jì,
and upon meeting said:
"Hé Lǘ is tyrannical,
as the prince knows.
Now he has slaughtered my wife and children,
burned them in the marketplace,
executing the innocent.
Regarding the affairs of Wú,
I know the inside story,
and wish to rely on the prince's courage,
so that Hé Lǘ can be captured.
Why not join me in going east to Wú?"
Qìng Jì believed his plan.
Three months later,
he selected and trained soldiers,
and then set out for Wú.
As they were about to cross the river,
in midstream,
Yāo Lí, being of slight strength,
positioned himself upwind,
and using the wind's force, hooked Qìng Jì's cap with his spear,
thrusting at Qìng Jì with the wind.
Qìng Jì turned and flung him away,
dunking his head into the water three times,
then placed him on his knee:
"Alas!
This is a warrior of the world,
who dares to raise a weapon against me."
His attendants wanted to kill him,
but Qìng Jì stopped them, saying:
"This is a warrior of the world;
how can we kill two such warriors in a single day!"
Then he instructed his attendants:
"Let him return to Wú,
to honor his loyalty."
Thereupon, Qìng Jì died.
Yāo Lí crossed to Jiānglíng,
but sorrowfully would not proceed.
His follower asked:
"Why do you not go on?"
Yāo Lí said:
"To have my wife and children killed,
in service to my lord,
is not benevolent.
To kill the former lord's son for a new lord,
is not righteous.
I value death,
but do not prize unrighteousness;
now that I cling to life and abandon integrity,
it is unrighteous.
To stand in the world with three evils,
what face have I to look upon the gentlemen of the world?"
Having spoken,
he threw himself into the river.
Before he drowned,
his follower pulled him out.
Yāo Lí said:
"How can I not die?"
The follower said:
"Do not die yet,
await your rank and emolument."
Yāo Lí then severed his own hands and feet,
and fell upon his sword to die.
In the third year,
the Wu general intended to attack Chu,
but had not yet launched the campaign.
Wǔ Zǐxū and Bó Xǐ said to each other:
"We have been cultivating talents for the king,
planning strategies,
all beneficial to the state,
yet the king proposes to attack Chu,
issuing the order,
but seems to entrust it without genuine intention to mobilize troops,
what should we do?"
After a while,
the King of Wú asked Wǔ Zǐxū and Bó Xǐ:
"I wish to send out troops,
what do you two think?"
Wǔ Zǐxū and Bó Xǐ replied:
"Your servants are willing to follow orders."
The King of Wú privately considered that both men bore grudges against Chu,
and deeply feared that sending troops would only lead to their destruction.
He ascended a terrace, faced the southern wind and whistled,
after a while sighed,
but none of the ministers understood the king's intent.
Wǔ Zǐxū, well aware of the king's indecision,
then recommended Sūnzǐ to the king.
This Sūnzǐ,
named Wǔ,
was a man of Wú.
He excelled in military strategy,
but lived in seclusion and withdrawal,
so no one in the world knew of his ability.
Zǐxū, with clear understanding and discerning judgment,
knew that Sūnzǐ could repel the enemy and eliminate threats.
Thus, one day while discussing military affairs with the King of Wú,
he recommended Sūnzǐ seven times.
The King of Wú said:
"Zǐxū's recommendation of a scholar
is meant to serve his own purposes."
Nevertheless, he summoned Sūnzǐ and questioned him about military strategy.
Each time he presented a section,
the king unconsciously praised it with his mouth,
his mind greatly pleased.
He asked:
"Can these military methods be tested on a small scale?"
Sūnzǐ said:
"Yes!
They can be tested with the women of the rear palace."
The king said:
"Agreed."
Sūnzǐ said:
"I request two of Your Majesty's favored concubines
to serve as unit leaders,
each commanding one team."
He ordered three hundred women to don armor and helmets,
grasp swords and shields and stand ready,
instructed them in military law,
to advance and retreat with the drumbeats,
turn left and right,
making them understand the prohibitions.
Then he commanded:
"At the first drum, all assemble;
at the second drum, advance with weapons;
at the third drum, assume battle formation."
Thereupon, the palace women all covered their mouths and laughed.
Sūnzǐ then personally took up the drumsticks and beat the drum,
repeated the orders multiple times,
yet their laughter continued as before.
Sūnzǐ looked back and saw the women laughing incessantly,
Sūnzǐ grew furious,
his eyes suddenly widened,
his voice like a terrifying tiger,
his hair stood up, lifting his cap,
the ties at his neck snapped,
he turned to the law officers and said:
"Bring the axes and execution blocks!"
Sūnzǐ said:
"If constraints are not clear,
commands are not trusted,
it is the general's fault.
Having already set the constraints,
repeated the orders multiple times,
if the soldiers still do not move accordingly,
it is the soldiers' error.
What does military law prescribe?"
The law officers said:
"Behead!"
Wǔ then ordered the beheading of the two unit leaders,
who were the King of Wú's favored concubines.
The King of Wú, watching from the terrace,
saw his two beloved concubines being executed,
swiftly sent a messenger down with the order:
"I already know the general's ability in employing troops.
Without these two concubines,
my food will have no flavor,
you should not behead them."
Sūnzǐ said:
"Your servant has already received the command to be general;
the general's law operates in the army;
even if the ruler gives an order,
your servant cannot accept it."
Sūnzǐ again beat the drum,
and they moved left and right, advanced and retreated,
turned with precision,
not daring to blink,
the two teams fell silent, none daring to look around.
Thereupon, he reported to the King of Wú:
"The troops are now well-ordered,
I wish Your Majesty to observe them.
Whatever you desire to use them for,
even sending them through fire and water,
will present no difficulty,
and thus you can stabilize the world."
The King of Wú suddenly became displeased,
saying:
"I know you are skilled in using troops,
and though this could lead to hegemony,
there is no way to implement it now.
General, dismiss the troops and return to your residence,
I have no further wish."
Sūnzǐ said:
"The king only likes the words but does not apply the reality."
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant hears that warfare is an inauspicious affair,
it cannot be tested idly.
Therefore, in military matters,
if executions and campaigns are not carried out,
the way of war remains unclear.
Now Your Majesty earnestly seeks capable men,
wishing to raise arms to punish the violent Chǔ,
to hegemonize the world and intimidate the feudal lords.
If not Sūn Wǔ as general,
then who can cross the Huái, surpass the Sì, traverse a thousand lǐ and wage war?"
Thereupon, the King of Wú was greatly pleased,
accordingly sounded the drums to assemble the army,
gathered them and attacked Chǔ.
With Sūnzǐ as general,
they captured Shū,
and killed the two rebel Wú generals, Gōngzǐ Gàiyú and Zhúyōng.
Planning to enter Yǐng,
Sūn Wǔ said:
"The people are weary, we cannot rely on them yet."
Chǔ heard that Wú had sent Sūnzǐ, Wǔ Zǐxū, and Bó Xǐ as generals,
Chǔ state suffered because of it,
all its ministers were resentful,
all saying Fèi Wújì had slandered and killed Wǔ Shē and Báizhōu Lí,
and Wú's invasion of their borders with unceasing raids,
caused the ministers of Chǔ to fear a sudden disaster.
At this time,
Sīmǎ Chéng said to Zǐcháng:
"Grand Tutor Wǔ Shē and Left Assistant Báizhōu Lí,
the people of the state did not know their crimes,
you and the king plotted to kill them,
spreading slander throughout the state,
to this day,
the talk has not ceased,
truly perplexing.
I have heard that even a benevolent person would not kill others to cover slander,
yet now you kill people to stir slander in the state,
is that not strange?
Fèi Wújì is the slanderous mouth of Chǔ,
the people do not know his faults.
Now, innocently killing three worthy men,
has incurred the enmity of Wú.
Internally, it wounds the hearts of loyal ministers;
externally, it makes us laughed at by neighboring states.
Moreover, the Xì and Wǔ families have fled to Wú,
Wú newly has Wǔ Yuán and Bó Xǐ,
wielding authority and determined,
bearing grudges against Chǔ,
thus the troops of our powerful enemy grow more alarming daily.
If Chǔ state faces trouble,
you will be in danger.
The wise remove slanderers to secure themselves,
the foolish accept flatterers to court their own ruin.
Now you accept slander,
the state is thereby endangered."
Zǐcháng said:
"This is Wǎ's fault,
dare I not plan to address it?"
In the ninth month,
Zǐcháng and King Zhāo together executed Fèi Wújì,
then exterminated his clan,
and the state's slander ceased.
The King of Wú had a daughter, Téng Yù,
while planning to attack Chǔ,
he dined on steamed fish with his wife and daughter,
the king first tasted half and gave it to his daughter,
the daughter angrily said:
"The king eating fish insults me,
I do not wish to live long."
Then she committed suicide.
Hélǘ grieved for her,
buried her west of the state outside the Chāng Gate.
He dug a pond, piled earth,
used patterned stone for the outer coffin,
placed a protective enclosure in the middle,
with treasures of gold tripods, jade cups, silver goblets, pearl garments,
all sent with the girl.
Then he had white cranes dance in the Wú market,
ordering the myriad people to follow and watch them,
Upon returning,
he had men, women, and cranes enter the tomb passage together,
then triggered the mechanism to seal them inside.
Killing the living to accompany the dead
was criticized by the people of the state.
The sword Zhànlú detested Hé Lü's lack of virtue,
so it left and went out,
traveling over water to Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Chǔ was lying down when he awoke,
and found the sword Zhànlú of the King of Wú by his bed.
King Zhāo did not know the reason for this,
so he summoned Fēng Húzǐ and asked:
"I awoke from lying down and obtained a precious sword,
but I do not know its name.
What sword is this?"
Fēng Húzǐ said:
"This is called the sword Zhànlú."
King Zhāo said:
"How can you tell?"
Fēng Húzǐ said:
"I have heard that the King of Wú obtained three precious swords presented by Yuè:
one called Yúcháng,
the second called Pányǐng,
and the third called Zhànlú.
The sword Yúcháng was already used to kill King Liáo of Wú,
Pányǐng was used to accompany his deceased daughter,
and now Zhànlú has come to Chǔ."
King Zhāo said:
"Why did Zhànlú leave?"
Fēng Húzǐ said:
"I have heard that King Yǔncháng of Yuè had Ōu Yězǐ forge five swords,
which were shown to Xuē Zhú.
Zhú responded:
'The sword Yúcháng goes against reason and is not harmonious;
it cannot be wielded properly.
A minister would use it to kill his ruler,
a son to kill his father.'
Therefore, Hé Lü used it to kill King Liáo.
Another named Pányǐng,
also called Háocáo,
is an object that does not follow the law,
of no benefit to people,
so it was used to accompany the dead.
Another named Zhànlú,
the essence of the five metals,
the quintessence of the Great Yang,
imbued with vital energy and entrusted with spirit,
emerges with divine presence,
and when wielded, it commands awe,
capable of repelling enemies and resisting foes.
However, if a ruler has plans that go against reason,
the sword will leave,
thus departing from the unvirtuous to join the virtuous.
Now the King of Wú is without virtue,
having killed his ruler and plotted against Chǔ,
so Zhànlú has come to Chǔ."
King Zhāo said:
"What is its value?"
Fēng Húzǐ said:
"I have heard that when this sword was in Yuè,
a guest offered its price:
thirty market towns, a thousand fine horses, and two cities of ten thousand households—
that was one offer.
Xuē Zhú responded:
'The mountain Chìjǐn has already been made cloudless,
the ravine of Ruòyē is deep and unfathomable;
the officials have ascended to heaven,
and Ōu Yě has died.'
Even if one were to offer a city's worth of gold,
fill rivers with pearls and jade,
one still could not obtain this treasure.
How much less could market towns, a thousand fine horses, and cities of ten thousand households
be worth mentioning?"
King Zhāo was greatly pleased,
and thus considered it a treasure.
Hé Lü heard that Chǔ had obtained the sword Zhànlú,
and because of this, he became enraged,
sending Sūn Wǔ, Wǔ Xū, and Bái Xǐ to attack Chǔ.
Zǐxū secretly ordered a proclamation to be spread in Chǔ:
"If Chǔ uses Zǐqī as general,
I will capture and kill him.
If Zǐcháng commands the troops,
I will withdraw."
Upon hearing this, Chǔ
thus used Zǐcháng
and dismissed Zǐqī.
Wú captured the two cities of Lù and Qián.
In the fifth year,
the King of Wú, because Yuè had not joined in attacking Chǔ,
attacked Yuè in the south.
King Yǔncháng of Yuè said:
"Wú does not keep the covenant of previous days,
abandoning a state that paid tribute and received rewards,
and destroying its friendly relations."
Hé Lü did not agree with his words.
So he attacked
and broke through Zuǐlǐ.
In the sixth year,
King Zhāo of Chǔ sent Prince Náng Wǎ to attack Wú,
in retaliation for the battles of Qián and Lù.
Wú sent Wǔ Xū and Sūn Wǔ to strike back,
besieging them in Yùzhāng.
The King of Wú said:
"I wish to take advantage of the danger to enter the capital of Chǔ and destroy its city Yǐng.
If we do not enter Yǐng,
what merit will you two have?"
Thereupon, they besieged the Chǔ army in Yùzhāng,
and greatly defeated them.
Then they besieged Cháo,
and captured it.
They captured Prince Fán of Chǔ and returned with him,
holding him as a hostage.
In the ninth year,
King of Wú said to Wǔ Zǐxū and Sūn Wǔ:
"Initially, you said Yǐng could not be captured,
so how does it turn out now?"
The two generals replied:
"In warfare,
relying on borrowed victories to establish one's might
is not the constant way to victory."
The King of Wú asked:
"What do you mean by that?"
The two generals said:
"Chǔ's military forces
are the strongest adversaries in the world.
Now if we contend with them head-on,
nine out of ten would perish with only one surviving,
and if Your Majesty enters Yǐng,
it would be due to Heaven's will.
We dare not guarantee it."
The King of Wú said:
"I wish to attack Chǔ again,
how can we achieve success?"
Wǔ Zǐxū and Sūn Wǔ said:
"Náng Wǎ
is greedy and has offended many feudal lords,
so Táng and Cài resent him.
If Your Majesty must attack,
what resentment would there be in gaining Táng and Cài's support?"
The two generals continued:
"Previously, Duke Zhāo of Cài paid homage to Chǔ,
having two fine fur coats and two excellent jade pendants,
he presented one of each to King Zhāo.
The king wore them to court,
while Duke Zhāo wore one set himself.
Zǐ Chǎng desired them,
but Duke Zhāo refused to give them.
Zǐ Chǎng detained him for three years, not allowing him to return to his state.
Duke Chéng of Táng paid homage to Chǔ,
having two patterned horses,
Zǐ Chǎng desired them,
but the duke refused to give them,
and was also detained for three years.
The ministers of Táng conspired together,
persuading the duke's attendants to offer the horses
to ransom Duke Chéng.
They gave wine to the attendants,
made them drunk,
stole the horses, and presented them to Zǐ Chǎng,
who then released Duke Chéng to return to his state.
The ministers criticized, saying:
'My lord, for the sake of a horse,
imprisoned yourself for three years;
we wish to reward the merit of stealing the horse.'
Thereupon,
Duke Chéng often thought of taking revenge on Chǔ,
and the ruler and ministers never ceased discussing it.
The people of Cài heard of this,
and insisted on presenting the fur coat and pendant to Zǐ Chǎng,
so Marquis Cài could return.
He went to Jìn to plead his case,
sent Zǐ Yuán and the crown prince as hostages,
and requested an attack on Chǔ.
Thus it is said,
with Táng and Cài, we can attack Chǔ."
The King of Wú then sent envoys to Táng and Cài, saying:
"Chǔ acts without principle,
cruelly killing loyal and good officials,
encroaching upon and devouring the feudal lords,
oppressing and humiliating your two lords.
I wish to raise troops to attack Chǔ,
and hope you two lords have a plan."
The Marquis of Táng sent his son Qián as a hostage to Wú,
and the three states conspired to attack Chǔ.
They stationed troops at Huáiruì,
and from Yùzhāng faced Chǔ across the Hàn River, forming battle lines.
Zǐ Chǎng then crossed the Hàn and arrayed his forces,
from Mount Xiǎobié to Mount Dàbié,
suffering three defeats,
he knew he could not advance,
and wanted to flee.
Shǐ Huáng said:
"Now Zǐ Chǎng, without reason, together with the king, killed three loyal ministers;
heaven's calamity descends,
caused by the king."
Zǐ Chǎng did not respond.
In the tenth month,
the two Chǔ armies arrayed at Bǎijǔ,
Fūgài, younger brother of Hé Lǘ, rose at dawn and requested of Hé Lǘ:
"Zǐ Chǎng is unvirtuous,
greedy and lacking in kindness,
his subordinates have no will to die;
if we pursue, we will surely defeat them."
Hé Lǘ did not permit it.
Fūgài said:
"This is what is called a subject acting on his own resolve without awaiting orders,
it refers to this situation."
Thereupon, he led his own troops of five thousand to attack Zǐ Chǎng,
greatly defeating him,
Zǐ Chǎng fled to Zhèng,
and the Chǔ army fell into great chaos.
The Wú army took advantage of this,
and thus crushed the Chǔ forces.
Before the Chǔ troops could cross the Hàn,
it happened that the Chǔ soldiers were eating,
and Wú rushed in and defeated them.
After five battles at Yōngzhì,
they advanced directly to Yǐng.
The king was pursued by the Wú invaders,
fleeing in desperation,
he escaped with his younger sister Jì Mǐ to the area between the Hé and Suī rivers,
the Chǔ senior official Yǐn Gù accompanied the king in the same boat.
The Wú army then entered Yǐng,
seeking King Zhāo.
The king crossed the Suī and then the Jiāng River,
entering Yúnzhōng.
At dusk, while resting,
a group of bandits attacked him,
striking the king's head with a dagger-axe;
Senior official Yǐn Gù shielded the king,
taking the blow on his back,
it hit his shoulder.
The king, terrified,
fled to Yún.
Senior official Zhǒng Jiàn carried Jì Mǐ on his back, following.
Duke Xīn of Yún found King Zhāo,
was overjoyed,
and wanted to return him.
His younger brother Huái angrily said:
"King Zhāo is our enemy."
He wanted to kill him,
saying to his elder brother Xīn:
"In the past, King Píng killed our father;
if I kill his son,
is that not fitting?"
Xīn said:
"When a ruler punishes his subject,
how dare one treat him as an enemy?
To take advantage of another's misfortune
is not benevolent.
To exterminate the ancestral line and abolish sacrifices
is not filial.
To act without a good reputation
is not wise."
Huái's anger did not subside.
Xīn secretly, with his youngest brother Cháo, took the king to Suí.
The Wú troops pursued them,
and said to the ruler of Suí:
"The descendants of Zhōu along the Hàn River,
Chǔ has exterminated them.
Heaven is said to repay such calamities,
inflicting punishment on Chǔ;
why do you treasure him?
What crime has the Zhōu house committed that you hide their enemy?
If you can hand over King Zhāo,
that would be a great kindness."
The ruler of Suí divined about King Zhāo and the King of Wú,
the omens were not auspicious,
so he declined to the King of Wú, saying:
"Now Suí is remote and small,
closely situated to Chǔ,
Chǔ has indeed preserved us,
our covenant remains unaltered to this day.
If we abandon them now in their difficulty,
and when all is peaceful again,
would Chǔ dare not obey your command?"
The Wú army, impressed by his words,
withdrew.
At that time,
although senior official Zǐqī was fleeing with King Zhāo,
he secretly made a deal with the Wú army,
intending to hand over the king.
The king learned of this,
and managed to escape,
then cut out Zǐqī's heart to swear a covenant with the ruler of Suí before leaving.
The King of Wú entered Yǐng,
and stayed there.
Wǔ Zǐxū, unable to capture King Zhāo,
dug up King Píng's tomb,
dragged out his corpse,
whipped it three hundred times,
then stepped on its belly with his left foot,
and gouged out its eyes with his right hand.
He cursed it, saying:
"Who made you use slanderous and flattering words,
to kill my father and brother?
Is this not unjust!"
He then ordered Hé Lǘ to take King Zhāo's wife as his own,
Wǔ Zǐxū, Sūn Wǔ, and Bái Xǐ also took the wives of Zǐ Chǎng and Minister of War Chéng,
thus humiliating the ruler and ministers of Chǔ.
They then led the army to attack Zhèng.
Duke Dìng of Zhèng had earlier killed Crown Prince Jiàn and persecuted Wǔ Zǐxū.
From then on, Duke Dìng of Zhèng was greatly afraid,
and issued a decree throughout the state:
"Whoever can make the Wú army withdraw,
I will share the rule of the state with him."
The son of a fisherman answered the call:
"I can make them withdraw,
without using a single soldier or a peck of grain,
just with an oar, singing on the road,
and they will withdraw."
The lord then took the oar from the fisherman's son.
As Wǔ Zǐxū's army approached,
he blocked the way, tapping the oar and singing:
"Reed dweller!"
He repeated this twice.
Hearing this,
Wǔ Zǐxū was startled and greatly alarmed,
asking:
"Who is it?"
He spoke to him:
"Who are you, sir?"
The reply came:
"I am the fisherman's son.
Our sovereign is terrified,
and has decreed throughout the state:
Whoever can make the Wú army withdraw
will share the kingdom and rule with him.
I recall how my father met you on the road,
and now I ask you for the state of Zhèng."
Wǔ Zǐxū sighed and said:
"How sorrowful!
I received the kindness of your father,
which brought me to this position.
Under the vast heavens above,
how could I dare forget it?"
Thereupon,
he spared the state of Zhèng,
withdrew his troops to guard against Chǔ,
and intensified his search for King Zhāo's whereabouts day by day.
Shēn Bāoxū had fled into the mountains;
upon hearing this,
he sent a messenger to tell Wǔ Zǐxū:
"Your vengeance
has gone too far!
You
were once a minister of King Píng,
personally served him facing north,
yet now you inflict the humiliation of desecrating his corpse—
is this not the extreme of immorality?"
Wǔ Zǐxū replied:
"Please convey my words to Shēn Bāoxū:
'As twilight falls and the road is long,
one stumbles and acts contrary on the path.'"
Realizing persuasion was futile,
Shēn Bāoxū went to Qín,
seeking aid for Chǔ.
Traveling day and night,
his feet blistering and cracking,
he tore his robes to wrap his knees,
leaned like a crane and wept at the Qín court,
crying without cease for seven days and nights.
Duke Āi of Qín was often intoxicated,
neglecting state affairs.
Shēn Bāoxū wept and then sang:
"Wú acts without morality,
like a giant boar and long serpent,
devouring the central states,
coveting the world,
starting their conquest with Chǔ.
My lord wanders in the wilderness,
sending me to plead for urgent help."
After seven days of this,
Duke Āi was greatly astonished:
"If Chǔ has such a worthy minister,
yet Wú still seeks to destroy it,
and I have no minister like this,
my downfall may be imminent!"
He then recited the poem "No Clothes":
"How can we say we have no clothes?
We'll share our robes with you.
The king is raising his army,
we'll share your enmity too."
Shēn Bāoxū responded:
"I hear that vicious virtue is insatiable;
if you, king, do not worry about the troubles on your neighbor's borders,
and while Wú is still unstable,
you do not seize your share,
if Chǔ perishes,
what benefit is that to Qín?
It would mean the loss of your land too.
I beg you, with your divine power, to preserve us,
and we will serve you for generations."
The earl of Qín sent a refusal,
saying:
"I have heard your plea;
please go to the guesthouse,
and I will deliberate and inform you."
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"My lord is now in the wilds,
with no place to rest;
how dare I seek comfort?"
He stood again in the court,
leaning against the wall and weeping,
his cries unceasing day and night,
without taking a sip of water.
Moved to tears,
the earl of Qín immediately dispatched troops to escort him back.
In the tenth year,
the Qin army had not yet set out,
when King Yǔncháng of Yuè, resentful of Hé Lǘ's earlier defeat of him at Zuìlǐ,
raised troops to attack Wú.
Wú's forces were in Chǔ,
and Yuè took the opportunity to launch a surprise attack on them.
In the sixth month,
