Shēn Bāoxū arrived with the Qin army,
dispatched by Qin under the command of Prince Zǐ Pú and Zǐ Hǔ with five hundred chariots,
to rescue Chǔ and strike Wú.
The two commanders said:
"We are unfamiliar with Wú's tactics."
They had the Chǔ army advance first to engage Wú in battle,
and then joined them at Jì,
decisively defeating Fū Gài.
In the seventh month,
Chǔ's Minister of War Zǐ Chéng and Qin's Prince Zǐ Pú faced off against the King of Wú,
while secretly sending a detachment to attack Táng,
and annihilated it.
Wǔ Zǐxū remained in Chǔ searching for King Zhāo,
refusing to leave.
Fū Gài's army was defeated and retreated.
In the ninth month,
he secretly returned,
and proclaimed himself King of Wú.
Hé Lǘ heard of this,
and immediately abandoned the campaign against Chǔ,
intending to kill Fū Gài.
Fū Gài fled to Chǔ,
where King Zhāo enfeoffed him at Tángxī.
Hé Lǘ then returned.
Wǔ Zǐxū, Sūn Wǔ, and Bái Xǐ remained,
and defeated the Chǔ army at Huáishì.
The Qin army again defeated the Wú forces,
and Chǔ's Zǐ Qī planned to set fire to the Wú army.
Zǐ Xī said:
"Our country's fathers and brothers have fought and their bones lie exposed in the wilds,
uncollected,
and now you would burn them too?
Is that acceptable?"
Zǐ Qī replied:
"When a state falls and loses its people,
what matters is survival or extinction;
why spare the dead at the cost of the living?
If the dead have consciousness,
they will surely ride the smoke and rise to aid us.
If they are without consciousness,
why begrudge the bones in the grass,
and let Wú escape destruction?"
So they set the fire and fought,
and the Wú army was severely defeated.
Wǔ Zǐxū and the others said to each other:
"Although Chǔ has defeated our remaining troops,
they have not truly harmed us."
Sūn Wǔ said:
"With Wú's arms, we have marched west to crush Chǔ,
driven out King Zhāo and desecrated King Jīng of Chǔ's tomb,
lacerating his corpse;
that is enough."
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"Since the age of Hegemons and Kings began,
no subject has ever avenged a wrong to this extent.
Let us go now!"
After the Wú army departed,
King Zhāo returned to his state.
The court musician Hùzǐ criticized the King of Chǔ for trusting slanderers,
executing Wǔ Shē and Bái Zhōulí,
leading to unending invasions on the border,
until finally the desecration of King Píng's tomb and the lashing of his corpse,
and the shame inflicted upon the rulers and ministers of Chǔ;
he also lamented King Zhāo's distress and peril,
nearly becoming the great laughingstock of the world,
and indeed already disgraced.
So he took up his lute and composed for Chǔ the song "Plights and Calamities,"
to express the sovereign's hardship and constrained plight.
The lyrics said:
"O king, O king,
how wayward and extreme,
disregarding the ancestral temple, heeding slanderous evil.
Employing Wújì, many were slain,
the Bái clan nearly exterminated by execution.
Two sons fled east to Wú and Yuè,
the King of Wú grieved and shared their sorrow.
With tears raised troops to march west and attack,
Wǔ Xū, Bái Xǐ, Sūn Wǔ decisive.
Three battles broke Yǐng, the king fled in haste,
lingering troops, unleashed cavalry, plundered the Chǔ court.
Chǔ's skeletons were exhumed and desecrated,
whips shamed the rotting corpse, disgrace hard to cleanse.
Ancestral temple nearly lost, state altars destroyed,
what crime had King Yán that his line almost ended?
Ministers mourn, people grieve in anguish,
though Wú's army left, fear does not cease.
I pray the king reforms, comforts the loyal and steadfast,
do not let slanderous mouths defile and blaspheme."
King Zhāo shed tears,
deeply understanding the lute song's sentiment,
and Hùzǐ never played it again.
Wǔ Zǐxū and the others passed by the waters of Lìyáng Lài,
and he sighed deeply, saying:
"I once starved here,
and begged food from a maiden;
she fed me,
then threw herself into the water and died."
He wished to repay her with a hundred pieces of gold but did not know her home,
so he threw the gold into the water and left.
After a while,
an old woman came walking and weeping;
someone asked her:
"Why do you weep so sorrowfully?"
The old woman said:
"I had a daughter,
who remained chaste at home until thirty unwed;
in past years she was beating silk here,
met a gentleman in dire straits and fed him,
but feared the matter would be exposed,
and threw herself into the Lài waters.
Now I hear Lord Wǔ has come,
but she received no recompense,
I grieve her death in vain,
hence my sorrow."
The person said:
"Wǔ Zǐxū wished to repay a hundred gold pieces,
but not knowing her home,
he threw the gold into the water and left."
The old woman then retrieved the gold and returned home.
Wǔ Zǐxū returned to Wú,
and the King of Wú heard that the three commanders were arriving,
prepared fish as kuài.
On the day they were to arrive,
they were overdue and did not come,
and the fish spoiled.
Shortly after,
Wǔ Zǐxū arrived,
Hé Lǘ brought out the kuài and ate it,
unaware of the foul smell.
The king had it made again,
and the taste was as before.
The people of Wú who make kuài
trace it back to Hé Lǘ's creation.
After the generals returned from Chǔ,
they renamed the Chāng Gate as the "Gate of Crushing Chǔ."
They again planned to attack Qí,
and Qí sent a daughter as a hostage to Wú,
so the King of Wú had his son, Prince Bō, betroth the Qí maiden.
The young maiden longed for Qí,
weeping day and night,
and thus fell ill.
Hé Lǘ then built the North Gate,
naming it the "Gate of Gazing toward Qí,"
and had the maiden stroll upon it.
Her longing did not cease,
her illness grew daily worse,
until she passed away.
The maiden said:
"If the dead have consciousness,
bury me atop Yú Mountain's peak,
to gaze upon Qí."
Hé Lǘ grieved for her,
and complied with her words,
burying her on Yú Mountain's summit.
At that time,
the crown prince also fell ill and died.
Hé Lǘ deliberated on choosing among the princes one to establish,
but had not decided.
Prince Bō's son, Fūchāi, day and night pleaded with Wǔ Xū:
"The king wishes to establish a crown prince;
if not I, then who should be established?
This plan rests with you, my lord."
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"The crown prince is not yet decided,
but when I enter, it will be settled."
Hé Lǘ soon summoned Wǔ Zǐxū to discuss establishing the crown prince,
and Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"I have heard that sacrifices cease without heirs,
and revive with descendants.
Now the crown prince has died untimely,
early bereft of service;
if the king wishes to establish a crown prince now,
none is more fitting than Fūchāi, son of Bō."
Hé Lǘ said:
"Fūchāi is foolish and unkind,
I fear he cannot uphold the lineage of Wú."
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"Fūchāi is trustworthy and benevolent,
upright in maintaining integrity,
sincere in ritual and righteousness.
A father dies, the son succeeds—
this is the clear text of the classics."
Hé Lǘ said:
"I follow you."
He established Fūchāi as crown prince,
and had the crown prince garrison troops to guard against Chǔ, remaining there.
He himself built palaces,
erected an archery tower in Ānlǐ,
with Huá Pool in Píngchāng,
and the Southern City Palace in Chánglè.
Hé Lǘ came and went, traveling and residing there.
In autumn and winter, governance was conducted within the city walls,
while in spring and summer, it took place outside the city.
He built the Gūsū Tower,
breakfasted at Qiū Shān,
and roamed the Sū Tower by day.
He shot arrows at Ōubēi,
galloped at Yóutái.
He enjoyed pleasures at Shíchéng,
hunted with hounds at Chángzhōu.
Such were the days of Hé Lǘ's hegemony.
Then the crown prince was settled,
and they attacked Chǔ,
crushing the army and capturing Pó.
Fearing the Wú troops would return,
Chǔ abandoned Yǐng.
They moved to Wěiruò.
At this time,
through the strategies of Wǔ Zǐxū, Bó Xǐ, and Sūn Wǔ,
Wú defeated the powerful Chǔ in the west,
intimidated Qí and Jìn in the north,
and campaigned against Yuè in the south.
In the eleventh year,
Fūchāi campaigned north against Qí,
and Qí sent the senior official Gāo to apologize to the Wú army, saying:
"Qí stands isolated as a small state,
with empty storehouses,
and its people scattered.
Qí regards Wú as a strong supporter,
yet before we could report our distress,
Wú has attacked us.
We beg to submit our people in the outskirts,
not daring to speak of war,
only hoping Wú will pity Qí for not overstepping."
The Wú army then withdrew.
In the twelfth year,
Fūchāi again campaigned north against Qí.
The King of Yuè heard of this,
led his followers to pay homage in Wú,
and presented lavish treasures to Grand Steward Pǐ,
who gladly accepted Yuè's bribes.
He grew exceptionally fond and trusting of Yuè,
speaking on their behalf day and night to the King of Wú.
The king trusted and employed Pǐ's schemes,
causing Wǔ Zǐxū great alarm.
He said:
"This is to abandon us."
So he went to admonish, saying:
"As for Yuè,
it is a disease in the heart and belly.
If we do not first remove this ailment,
but now believe in empty words and deceit while coveting Qí,
even if we defeat Qí,
it would be like cultivating a field of solid rock—
no seedlings will take root.
I urge Your Majesty to forsake Qí and confront Yuè first.
Otherwise,
regret will be too late."
The King of Wú did not listen,
instead sending Zǐxū as an envoy to Qí,
to arrange the scheduled battle meeting.
Zǐxū told his son:
"I have repeatedly advised the king,
but he does not heed me.
Now I foresee Wú's downfall.
If you perish with me,
it would be in vain."
So he entrusted his son to the Bào family of Qí and returned.
Grand Steward Pǐ, bearing a grudge against Zǐxū,
slandered him, saying:
"Zǐxū forces his advice through strength;
I hope Your Majesty will show him little favor."
The king said:
"I am aware."
Before raising the army,
it happened that Lǔ sent Zǐgòng on a mission to Wú.
In the thirteenth year,
Chéng Héng, a senior official of Qí, intended to assassinate Duke Jiǎn,
but secretly feared the Gāo, Guó, Bào, and Yàn families,
so he first raised an army to attack Lǔ.
The ruler of Lǔ was deeply troubled by this.
Confucius was also concerned,
and summoned his disciples to tell them:
"When states attack each other,
I have always felt ashamed.
Now Lǔ,
the land of my ancestors,
where my ancestral tombs lie,
is about to be invaded by Qí.
Would none of you consider going out to intervene?"
Zǐlù volunteered to go out,
but Confucius stopped him.
Zǐzhāng and Zǐshí then offered to go,
but Confucius did not permit them.
When Zǐgòng volunteered to go out,
Confucius sent him.
Zǐgòng went north to Qí,
met with Chéng Héng,
and said to him:
"Lǔ
is a state difficult to attack,
yet you, sir, are attacking it -
this is a mistake."
Chéng Héng said:
"Why is Lǔ difficult to attack?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Its city walls are low and thin,
its moats narrow and shallow,
its ruler foolish and unkind,
its high ministers hypocritical and incompetent,
and its people detest warfare -
these are reasons not to fight them.
You would be better off attacking Wú.
For Wú
has high, thick walls,
wide and deep moats,
armored soldiers carefully selected,
weapons well-maintained and crossbows powerful,
with capable ministers guarding it -
this makes it easy to attack."
Chéng Héng flushed with anger
and said:
"What you call difficult,
others find easy;
what you call easy,
others find difficult.
And you advise Héng thus -
why?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have heard that you attempted three times to gain fiefs but failed each time
because some ministers would not obey you.
Now you wish to destroy Lǔ to expand Qí's territory,
demolish Lǔ to enhance your own status,
yet you gain no merit from this -
this shows you inflate the ruler's arrogance above,
and indulge the ministers below,
while seeking to achieve great things -
this is difficult.
Moreover, when superiors become arrogant they offend,
when ministers become arrogant they contend -
this means you have conflicts with the ruler above,
and disputes with ministers below.
In such circumstances,
your position in Qí
is as precarious as piled eggs.
Therefore I say you should attack Wú instead.
Besides, the King of Wú is resolute and determined,
able to enforce his commands,
his people accustomed to warfare and defense,
his generals well-versed in laws and prohibitions -
if Qí encounters them, you will certainly be captured,
without doubt.
Now if you mobilize all within your borders,
send out your ministers to surround them,
your people will die abroad,
your ministers be depleted at home,
leaving you without strong ministers above to oppose the enemy,
nor common people below to support you -
the one who controls Qí while isolating the ruler
would be you, sir."
Chéng Héng said:
"Well said.
However,
my troops are already at Lǔ's city walls.
If I withdraw to attack Wú,
my ministers will suspect my intentions -
what should I do about this?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Hold your troops and do not attack,
allow me to go south to see the King of Wú,
to request he rescue Lǔ and attack Qí,
then you can lead your troops to meet them."
Chéng Héng agreed.
Zǐgòng went south to see the King of Wú,
and told the King of Wú:
"I have heard that
a true king does not let states perish,
and a hegemon has no powerful enemies.
A weight of thousand jūn can be moved by adding tiny amounts.
Now with mighty Qí of ten thousand chariots taking private possession of Lǔ with its thousand chariots,
and competing with Wú for supremacy,
I secretly fear for you, my lord.
Moreover, rescuing Lǔ
brings fame;
attacking Qí
brings great benefit.
Righteously preserving perishing Lǔ,
actually harming violent Qí and intimidating powerful Jìn -
this leaves no doubt about your kingship."
The King of Wú said:
"Well said.
However,
I once fought Yuè,
drove them to Kuàijī,
made them submit to Wú,
but did not execute them immediately.
After three years I sent them back.
The ruler of Yuè is a worthy lord,
who hardens his body and labors strenuously,
working day and night,
improving governance internally,
dealing with other states externally -
he must be planning revenge against me.
Wait until I attack Yuè, then I will follow your advice."
Zǐgòng said:
"That won't do.
Yuè's strength does not exceed Lǔ's,
Wú's strength does not exceed Qí's.
If you attack Yuè instead of following my advice,
Qí will have already taken Lǔ.
Moreover, fearing small Yuè while resenting powerful Qí
shows lack of courage.
Seeing small gains while forgetting great dangers
shows lack of wisdom.
I have heard that benevolent people do not let difficulties hinder their virtue's expansion,
wise people do not miss opportunities to achieve merit,
true kings do not let states perish to establish their righteousness.
Since you fear Yuè so much,
allow me to go east to see the King of Yuè,
to have him send troops to follow your command."
The King of Wú was greatly pleased.
Zǐgòng went east to see the King of Yuè,
who, upon hearing of his arrival,
cleared the roads and welcomed him at the outskirts,
personally escorted him to his residence and asked:
"This remote, narrow state with its barbarian people -
why has you, sir, come so solemnly without feeling insulted,
to reach this place?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I came because of your situation."
Yuè King Gōu Jiàn bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
saying:
"I have heard that
misfortune and fortune are neighbors,
now that you, sir, come to comfort me,
this is my fortune.
How dare I not ask for your explanation?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I recently saw the King of Wú,
advised him to rescue Lǔ and attack Qí,
his mind was willing,
but his will fears Yuè.
Moreover, having no intention of revenge yet making others suspect you -
this is clumsy.
this is dangerous.
When matters are not yet initiated but become known -
this is perilous.
These three things
are major taboos for undertaking affairs."
The King of Yuè bowed again,
saying:
"I lost my predecessors young,
failed to measure myself properly,
fought against the people of Wú,
suffered military defeat and personal humiliation,
left shame for my ancestors,
fled in escape,
dwelling in Kuàijī above,
guarding the seaside below,
only seeing fish and turtles.
Now that you, sir, honor me with your visit and personally see me,
and speak precious words to instruct me,
this is heaven's gift to me.
How dare I not receive your teaching?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have heard that
enlightened rulers appoint people without wasting their abilities,
upright scholars recommend worthies undeterred by worldly opinions.
Thus for distributing wealth and benefits employ the benevolent,
for facing troubles and difficulties employ the courageous,
for using wisdom to plan for the state employ the worthy,
for rectifying the world and stabilizing the states employ the sagely.
If one has strong troops but cannot exercise their power,
holds high position but cannot implement governance below,"
Is the ruler of Yuè nearly ready?
It is difficult!
I have privately selected one who can achieve success and reach kingly status,
is it nearly me?
Now the King of Wú has ambitions to attack Qí and Jìn.
Do not spare precious vessels to please his heart,
nor disdain humble words to exhaust his courtesy,
and attack Qí,
Qí will certainly fight.
If they do not win,
it is your blessing;
if they fight and win,
they will surely lead their troops to confront Jìn.
With knights and sharp troops worn out by Qí,
and treasures, chariots, cavalry, and feathers exhausted by Jìn,
then you can control what remains. "
The King of Yuè bowed twice,
and said:
"In the past,
the King of Wú divided his numerous people to devastate our state,
killed and defeated our people,
humiliated our populace,
destroyed our ancestral temples,
turning the state into ruins and thorns,
and our bodies into fish and turtles.
My hatred for Wú
runs deeper than marrow;
yet my service to Wú
is like a son fearing his father,
or a younger brother respecting his elder.
This is my dying word.
Now that you, Great Officer, have bestowed advice,
how dare I harbor doubts?
Allow me to speak my mind:
I have not rested comfortably on thick mats,
my mouth has not tasted rich flavors,
my eyes have not beheld beautiful sights,
my ears have not listened to elegant music,
for three years already.
With parched lips and dry tongue,
tormenting my body and laboring with effort,
serving my ministers above,
nurturing the common people below,
I wish to engage Wú in battle once on the open plains of the world,
straightening my body and arms to strive;
if the men of Wú and Yuè fall in succession, with livers and brains smearing the ground,
it is my desire.
I have pondered this for three years,
but it has been unattainable.
Now, internally assessing, our state is insufficient to harm Wú,
externally, serving the other lords is not feasible.
I am willing to empty the state, abandon my ministers, change my appearance, alter my name, take up broom and dustpan, tend oxen and horses to serve them.
Though I know my neck and waist may be severed,
hands and feet separated,
limbs scattered,
laughed at by villages and towns,
my intent remains firm.
Now that you, Great Officer, have bestowed advice,
it is to preserve a perishing state and revive the dead,
I rely on the blessing of my ancestors,
how dare I not await your command? "
Zǐgòng said:
"The King of Wú's character
is greedy for achievement and fame but ignorant of gain and harm. "
The King of Yuè respectfully stepped aside from his position.
Zǐgòng said:
"I observe that the King of Wú engages in frequent campaigns,
his soldiers receive no kindness,
his great ministers are internally divided,
and slanderers multiply.
As for Wǔ Xū's character,
he is sincere and internally upright,
outwardly clear-sighted and aware of the times,
not concealing his ruler's faults even unto death,
speaking forthrightly to be loyal to his lord,
acting directly for the state's benefit,
yet his advice went unheeded until his death.
Grand Steward Pǐ's character,
is wise yet foolish,
strong yet weak,
using clever words and sharp speech to secure his position,
skilled in deceit to serve his lord,
knowing the present but ignorant of the future,
indulging his lord's errors to safeguard his private interests,
he is a treacherous minister who ruins the state and harms the ruler. "
The King of Yuè was greatly pleased.
Zǐgòng departed,
the King of Yuè presented him with a hundred yì of gold, a precious sword, and two fine horses,
but Zǐgòng did not accept.
Arriving in Wú,
he said to the King of Wú:
"I conveyed your subordinate's words to the King of Yuè,
and the King of Yuè was extremely frightened,
saying:
'In the past, I was unfortunate,
losing my predecessors early,
and internally, not knowing my measure,
offended Wú and incurred punishment.
My army defeated, myself disgraced,
I fled in escape,
taking refuge in Kuàijī,
my state turned to ruins and wilderness,
my body to fish and turtles.
Relying on Your Majesty's grace,
I was able to hold sacrificial vessels,
and perform rituals,
I would not dare forget even in death,
how dare I contemplate any schemes? '
His resolve is one of great fear,
and he will send an envoy to apologize to you. "
Zǐgòng stayed at the guesthouse for five days,
and a Yuè envoy indeed came,
saying:
"The envoy of Gòujiàn, your servant from the Eastern Sea, named Wén Zhǒng,
dares to address your subordinate,
and briefly inform your attendants:
In the past, I was unfortunate,
losing my predecessors early,
and internally, not knowing my measure,
offended your superior state and incurred punishment,
my army defeated, myself disgraced,
I fled in escape,
taking refuge in Kuàijī,
relying on your king's grace to perform sacrifices,
I would not forget even in death.
Now I have privately heard that Your Majesty will rise for a great righteousness,
to punish the strong and save the weak,
subdue the violent Qí and pacify the Zhōu court,
thus I send your humble servant to present the vessels stored by previous kings:
twenty sets of armor, the Qūlú spears, and Bùguāng swords,
to congratulate your army officers.
If you will pursue this great righteousness,
though our humble state is small,
we ask to muster three thousand soldiers from all within the four borders to follow your subordinate,
and I myself ask to don armor and wield weapons,
to advance and receive arrows and stones,
so that ruler and ministers may die without regret. "
The King of Wú was greatly pleased,
and summoned Zǐgòng, saying:
"The Yuè envoy has indeed come,
offering three thousand soldiers,
and their ruler will also join,
to assist me in attacking Qí,
is this acceptable? "
Zǐgòng said:
"It is not acceptable.
To empty another's state,
take all their people,
and also have their ruler accompany you,
is unrighteous.
Accept their gifts,
approve their troops,
but decline their ruler's participation,
that would be appropriate. "
The King of Wú agreed.
Zǐgòng left for Jìn,
and appearing before Duke Dìng, said:
"I have heard that
if plans are not set in advance,
one cannot respond to emergencies;
if troops are not prepared beforehand,
one cannot defeat the enemy.
Now Wú and Qí are about to fight,
if they fight and do not win,
Yuè will surely cause chaos.
If they fight and win,
they will surely lead their troops to confront Jìn,
what will you do, my lord? "
Duke Dìng said:
"How should we respond? "
Zǐgòng said:
"Train troops and set ambushes to await them. "
The ruler of Jìn agreed.
Zǐgòng returned to Lǔ,
and the King of Wú indeed raised troops from nine commaneries,
preparing to fight Qí.
Passing through Xūmén on the way,
he passed by Gūxū Tower,
and suddenly, taking a daytime nap at Gūxū Tower, he had a dream;
upon waking and rising,
his heart was calm yet troubled.
He then summoned Grand Steward Pǐ,
and said:
"I napped during the day and had a dream,
upon waking, I feel calm yet troubled.
I ask you to interpret it,
could it be that I have worries?
I dreamed of entering Zhāngmíng Palace,
saw two pots,
steaming but not cooking,
two black dogs barking to the south and barking to the north,
two spades planted by my palace walls,
flowing waters rushing,
passing through my palace hall,
in the back room, the sound of drums and boxes, with a blacksmith at work,
in the front garden, horizontal ropes and a paulownia tree growing.
Interpret this for me. "
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"Splendid!
Your Majesty's raising an army to attack Qí.
Your servant has heard that a 'zhāng' (insignia) signifies
virtue resounding splendidly.
A 'míng' (brightness) means
shattering the enemy with achievements clear and luminous.
Two pots of steaming grain left uncooked
indicate the Great King's sage virtue has surplus energy.
Two black dogs barking to the south and barking to the north
show the four barbarians are subdued,
and feudal lords come to court.
Two plowshares planted by the palace wall
mean farmers succeed in tilling the fields.
Torrential waters flowing through the palace hall
signify neighboring states offer tribute with abundant wealth.
The constant clanging of smiths from the rear chamber
shows palace maidens delight in harmonious lutes and zithers.
Crosswise ropes growing with parasol trees in the front garden
represent the Music Bureau's drumbeats."
King Wú was greatly pleased,
yet his mind remained unsettled.
He summoned Wángsūn Luò and asked:
"I suddenly had a daytime dream—
interpret it for me."
Wángsūn Luò replied:
"Your servant is crude and shallow in the Way,
unable to grasp its breadth.
Regarding the king's dream,
I cannot interpret it.
But there is one who knows—
Gōngsūn Shèng, younger brother of the Elder of Chángchéng at the East Side Gate pavilion.
Shèng in youth loved to wander,
in adulthood loved learning,
has seen much and observed widely,
knows the conditions of spirits and ghosts.
I beg the king to consult him."
The king then sent Wángsūn Luò to invite Gōngsūn Shèng,
saying:
"The King of Wú was napping on Gūxū Tower,
suddenly was moved by a dream,
awoke disconsolate,
and bids you interpret it.
Go quickly to Gūxū Tower."
Gōngsūn Shèng prostrated weeping,
after a while rose,
as his wife beside him said:
"How boorish your nature!
Rarely seeing your sovereign,
yet when urgently summoned,
you weep like pouring rain."
Gōngsūn Shèng looked up and sighed:
"Alas!
This is beyond your understanding.
Today is rénwǔ day,
the hour points south,
fate belongs to heaven—
I cannot escape.
My prostrate weeping
is not merely self-pity,
but truly grieves for the King of Wú."
His wife said:
"You should through the Way reach your lord,
practice the Way when needed,
admonish the king above,
restrain yourself below.
Now hearing urgent summons,
you're anxious and confused—
unbecoming a worthy man."
Gōngsūn Shèng said:
"Foolish
are a woman's words!
I've cultivated the Way ten years,
hidden to avoid harm,
hoping to live out my lifespan.
Unexpectedly summoned urgently,
abandoning myself mid-life—
hence I mourn parting from you."
He then left
for Gūxū Tower.
The King of Wú said:
"I plan to attack Qí and Lǔ northward,
passing through Xū Gate,
crossing Gūxū Tower,
when suddenly I dreamed by day.
Interpret it for me,
telling its good or ill."
Gōngsūn Shèng said:
"If I don't speak,
my body and name remain intact;
if I speak,
I'll die in pieces before the king.
But a loyal minister disregards his person."
Then looking up, he sighed:
"I've heard lovers of boats drown,
lovers of war perish.
I love straight speech,
regardless of life—
may the king consider this.
I hear 'zhāng' means
defeat in battle, fleeing in panic.
'Míng' means
leaving light for darkness.
Entering to see steamed grain uncooked
means the Great King won't get cooked meals.
Two black dogs barking south and north—
black signifies darkness,
north signifies concealment.
Two plowshares by the palace wall
mean Yuè troops entering Wú,
destroying ancestral temples,
digging up altars of land and grain.
Torrents flowing through the palace hall
mean the palace stands empty.
Constant clanging from the rear chamber
means sitting in deep sighs.
Crosswise ropes with parasol trees in front
—parasol wood is hollow-hearted,
useless for vessels,
only making blind boys' staffs
buried with the dead.
I beg the Great King to halt troops, cultivate virtue,
not attack Qí—
then this can be dispelled.
Send officers like Tàizǎi Pǐ and Wángsūn Luò
to bare shoulders, bare feet,
kowtow to Gōu Jiàn in apology—
then the state may be preserved,
and your life spared."
Hearing this, the King of Wú
flared in anger,
saying:
"I am born of heaven,
sent by spirits!"
He ordered strongman Shí Fān to beat him to death with an iron hammer.
Shèng looked up and cried to heaven:
"Alas!
Heaven knows my injustice!
Loyalty brings crime,
I die innocent.
Bury me—
better to take me as a post,
carry me to deep mountains,
that my voice may echo through ages!"
The King of Wú then had guards throw him into Zhēng Hill,
"Let wolves eat your flesh,
wildfires burn your bones!
East winds will blow repeatedly,
scattering your remains—
flesh and bones rotting,
how can your voice echo then?"
Tàizǎi Pǐ hurried forth:
"Congratulations, Great King—
the disaster is quelled.
Let us raise cups:
the army may march."
The King of Wú made Tàizǎi Pǐ Right Colonel Marshal,
Wángsūn Luò Left Colonel Marshal,
and followed Gōu Jiàn's troops to attack Qí.
Wǔ Zǐxū heard this
and admonished:
"I've heard raising a host of 100,000,
marching troops a thousand lǐ,
costs the people
and drains the state
thousands in gold daily.
Heedless of officers' and people's deaths,
contending for a day's victory—
I consider this utmost danger to state and life.
Moreover, dwelling with bandits,
unaware of the calamity,
seeking conflict abroad,
gambling on other states—
like treating scabies
while ignoring a fatal inner illness,
which will erupt fatally.
Scabies
are skin ailments,
not worth fearing.
Now Qí declines a thousand lǐ away,
beyond Chǔ and Zhào borders—
Qí as ailment
is but scabies.
Yuè as disease
is the fatal inner illness.
Untreated, it injures;
agitated, it kills.
I beg the Great King to secure Yuè before plotting against Qí.
My words are decisive—
dare I not be utterly loyal?
I am now aged,
ears and eyes dim,
with a confused heart,
unable to benefit the state.
I've privately observed the eighth chapter of the Golden Casket—
it is truly grievable."
The King of Wú said:
"What does it mean?"
Zǐxū said:
"This year, seventh month, xīnhài day at dawn,
the Great King initiates affairs.
Xīn
marks the year's position.
Hài is the hour preceding Yīn.
It combines with Rénzǐ year's pre-combination,
favorable for military campaigns.
Military action ensures victory,
yet virtue remains present.
Aligning with the Dipper strikes Chǒu,
Chǒu being the root of Xīn.
Dàjí as the White Tiger oversees Xīn,
while Gōngcáo as Tàicháng presides over Hài.
Dàjí obtaining Xīn forms the Nine Calamities,
further intensified by conjunction with the White Tiger.
Should anyone initiate affairs under this configuration,
though minor triumphs may come first,
great defeat will inevitably follow,
with heaven and earth unleashing calamities—
ruin approaches swiftly!"
The King of Wú disregarded this,
and in the ninth month dispatched Grand Steward Pǐ to attack Qí.
As the army reached the northern outskirts,
the king told Pǐ:
"Go forth,
never forget the meritorious,
nor pardon the guilty.
Cherish the people and nurture officers,
treating them as your own children.
Consult the wise in strategy,
befriend the benevolent."
Receiving these orders,
Grand Steward Pǐ departed.
The King of Wú then summoned Minister Bèi Lí,
asking:
"You have long shared convictions with Zǐxū,
jointly deliberating strategies.
Now that I raise armies against Qí,
what objections does Zǐxū alone voice?"
Bèi Lí replied:
"Zǐxū wishes to devote loyalty to the former king,
calling himself aged and insane,
with dimmed sight and hearing,
ignorant of contemporary governance,
thus of no use to Wú."
The king proceeded to attack Qí.
At Àilíng, Qí clashed with Wú,
and the Qí army suffered defeat.
Victorious, the King of Wú
sent an envoy to propose peace with Qí,
stating:
"Hearing Qí faced flooding threats,
our king came to observe.
Yet Qí mobilized troops in marshlands,
leaving Wú uncertain how to settle,
so we formed battle arrays defensively—
unintentionally harming Qí's forces.
We wish to establish alliance before withdrawal."
The King of Qí responded:
"I reside in these northern lands,
never plotting beyond borders.
Now Wú has crossed the Jiāng and Huái,
traversing a thousand lǐ to our soil,
slaughtering our people.
By heaven's mercy,
our state avoids collapse.
Since your king proposes peace,
how dare I refuse?"
Thus Wú and Qí covenanted before parting.
Returning, the King of Wú rebuked Zǐxū:
"Our former king practiced virtue,
his sagacity reaching heaven,
laboring to build achievements,
forging your western vengeance against Chǔ.
Like a farmer clearing wild weeds,
he earned fame among the Jīngmán tribes—
all through your efforts too.
Now you, in senile unrest,
breed turmoil and deceit,
venting malice abroad,
blaming our officers,
disrupting our laws,
seeking to hex our armies into defeat.
Yet heaven granted favor,
humbling Qí's forces.
How dare I claim credit?
It stems from our former king's legacy,
blessed by divine spirits.
What have you contributed to Wú?"
Wǔ Zǐxū rolled up sleeves in fury,
laying down his sword to retort:
"Our former king had ministers who dared dissent,
resolving doubts and averting evils,
thus escaping great perils.
Now you discard elders,
ignoring external threats—
this is a puppet's strategy,
unworthy of hegemony.
Heaven's abandonment begins
with chasing minor joys
while nearing major woes.
Should you awaken,
Wú may endure for generations;
if not, its fate shortens.
I cannot feign illness to flee,
witnessing your capture.
Should I die first,
hang my eyes upon the gate
to watch Wú's downfall."
The King of Wú ignored him.
Seated in his hall,
he saw four men back-to-back facing the courtyard.
Startled, he stared as ministers asked:
"What does Your Majesty see?"
He said:
"Four men leaning back-to-back—
they scatter at human speech."
Zǐxū said:
"This portends loss of popular support."
The king fumed:
"Your words are ill-omened."
Zǐxū replied:
"Not just ill-omened—
you will perish too."
Five days later,
the king again sat in hall,
spotting two men facing each other,
the northerner killing the southerner.
He asked ministers:
"Do you see?"
They said:
"Nothing."
Zǐxū inquired:
"What did you see?"
The king said:
"Like the four before,
but now two confronting—
northerner slaying southerner."
Zǐxū said:
"Four fleeing means rebellion;
northerner killing southerner means
minister assassinating ruler."
The king remained silent.
At a feast in Wéntái Palace,
all ministers present,
Grand Steward Pǐ governing,
the King of Yuè attending,
and Zǐxū among them,
the king declared:
"I hear: rulers never despise meritorious ministers,
nor fathers hate capable sons.
Now Pǐ has served me well—
I shall ennoble him with highest honors.
The King of Yuè, kind and faithful,
serves me with filial duty—
I will restore his lands
to reward his campaign aid.
What say you, ministers?"
They congratulated:
"Your Majesty embodies virtue,
humbly nurturing officers.
All ministers advance,
competing to die in crises,
your fame resplendent,
awe shaking the realm.
The merited receive rewards,
fallen states revive—
achievements of hegemony
all flow through your ministers."
Then Zǐxū knelt, weeping:
"Alas! Woe!
To endure such silence—
loyal ministers gagged,
slanderers favored;
governance ruined,
flattery unchecked;
crooked words
straighten falsehoods;
attacking loyalty for deceit—
this dooms Wú!
Ancestral temples razed,
altars neglected;
cities becoming wastes,
thorns sprouting in courts."
The King of Wú roared:
"This old minister schemes,
haunting Wú like a specter.
He craves authority,
seeking to overthrow us.
For our former king's sake,
I spared him punishment.
Now withdraw and reflect—
hinder not Wú's plans."
Zǐxū said:
"Now I am neither loyal nor trustworthy,
and cannot be considered a minister of the former king.
I dare not cherish my own life,
but I fear for Wúguó's impending downfall.
In ancient times, Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
Now if the great king executes me,
you would be comparable to Jié and Zhòu.
May the great king exert himself,
I beg to take my leave."
Zǐxū returned
and said to Bèilí:
"I crossed borders with bow and arrow between Zhèng and Chǔ,
traversed the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and reached this place of my own accord.
The former king listened to my strategies,
defeated Chǔ to avenge past humiliations.
I wished to repay the former king's kindness and thus reached this point.
It's not that I regret my own fate,
but disaster will soon befall you."
Bèilí said:
"If advice is not heeded,
what good is suicide?
Why not flee?"
Zǐxū said:
"Where would a fugitive minister go?"
When the King of Wú heard of Zǐxū's resentment,
he sent someone to present the Shǔlòu sword.
Zǐxū received the sword,
barefoot and lifting his robes,
descended to the central courtyard,
looked up to heaven crying out his grievance,
saying:
"I initially served your father as a loyal minister to establish Wú,
devised strategies to defeat Chǔ,
subdued the powerful Yuè in the south,
imposed authority over the various lords,
achieving hegemon's merit.
Now you disregard my counsel,
instead granting me this sword.
When I die today,
the Wú palace will become ruins,
the courtyard overgrown with weeds,
the Yuè people will dig up your altars of state.
How can you forget me?
Previously the former king did not wish to establish you,
I contended for you at the risk of my life,
ultimately fulfilling your wish;
the young lord harbors much resentment toward me.
I merely achieved merit for Wú,
now you forget my grace in stabilizing the state,
instead granting me death,
is this not absurd!"
The King of Wú heard this,
and angrily said:
"You are neither loyal nor trustworthy,
when serving as my envoy to Qí,
you entrusted your son to the Bào family of Qí,
harboring intentions against me."
He urgently ordered him to commit suicide.
"I will not let you see anything."
Zǐxū grasped the sword,
looked up to heaven and sighed:
"After my death,
later generations will certainly regard me as loyal.
Matching the eras of Xià and Yīn,
I will also join as a companion to Guān Lóngpáng and Bǐgān."
Then he fell on the sword and died.
The King of Wú took Zǐxū's corpse,
placed it in a leather sack,
and cast it into the river,
saying:
"Xū,
after your death,
what awareness can you have?"
Then he severed the head,
placed it on a high tower,
saying to it:
"The sun and moon will scorch your flesh,
the blowing wind will dry your eyes,
fiery light will burn your bones,
fish and turtles will eat your flesh,
your bones will turn to ash,
what will you be able to see?"
Then he discarded the body,
casting it into the river.
Zǐxū then rode the waves with the current,
moving with the tides,
surging to erode the banks.
Thereupon the King of Wú said to Bèilí:
"You once discussed my faults with Zǐxū."
Then he shaved Bèilí's head and punished him.
Wángsūn Luò heard of this,
and did not attend court.
The king summoned and asked him:
"Why do you criticize me and not attend court?"
Luò said:
"I am merely afraid!"
The king said:
"Do you consider my killing of Zǐxū significant?"
Luò said:
"The great king's authority is lofty,
Zǐxū's position was lowly,
yet the king executed him.
How is my life different from Zǐxū's?
This is why I am afraid."
The king said:
"It was not that I listened to Zǎipǐ to kill Zǐxū,
but that Xū was plotting against me."
Luò said:
"I have heard that a ruler
must have ministers who dare to remonstrate;
those in high positions
must have friends who dare to speak frankly.
As for Zǐxū,
he was a veteran minister of the former king.
If neither loyal nor trustworthy,
he could not have been a minister to the former king."
The King of Wú felt remorseful in his heart,
regretting Zǐxū's execution:
"Was it not Zǎipǐ who slandered Zǐxū?"
And he wished to kill him.
Luò said:
"That cannot be done.
If the king kills Pǐ,
this would be creating a second Zǐxū."
Thereupon he did not execute him.
In the fourteenth year,
after Fūchāi had killed Wǔ Zǐxū,
there were consecutive years of poor harvests,
and the people were full of resentment.
The King of Wú again attacked Qí,
digging a canal between Shāng and Lǔ,
connecting north to Qí
and west to Jǐ.
He intended to join Lǔ and Jìn in a joint attack at Huángchí.
Fearing that his ministers might remonstrate again,
he issued an order throughout the state:
"I am attacking Qí;
anyone who dares to remonstrate will die."
Crown Prince Yǒu knew that Zǐxū had been loyal but unused, while Grand Steward Pǐ was cunning and monopolized power.
He wished to speak bluntly,
but feared incurring blame,
so he used allegorical remonstrance to provoke the king.
At dawn, carrying pellets and a slingshot,
he came from the rear garden,
with his clothes drenched and shoes soaked.
The king, surprised, asked him:
"Why are your clothes drenched and shoes soaked,
and your body in such a state?"
Crown Prince Yǒu replied:
"I was just wandering in the rear garden,
heard the sound of autumn cicadas,
and went to observe them.
The autumn cicada climbs a high tree,
drinks the clear dew,
sways with the wind,
sings long and mournfully,
thinking itself secure.
Unaware that the mantis, leaping across branches and clinging to twigs,
dragging its waist and raising its claws,
is poised to strike its form.
The mantis, focused and advancing,
is intent on gain.
Unaware that the yellow sparrow fills the green woods,
hovering in the shade of branches,
subtly advancing,
aims to peck the mantis.
The yellow sparrow only knows to watch for the mantis as a tasty morsel,
unaware that I, gripping a slingshot and poised to throw,
with a swift flick, send a pellet to strike its back.
Now, I was solely intent on the yellow sparrow,
unaware of the empty pit beside, suddenly falling into it,
trapped in a deep well.
Thus, my body is drenched and shoes soaked,
nearly becoming a laughingstock for Your Majesty."
The king said:
"The folly in the world,
none surpasses this.
Only greedy for immediate gain,
blind to future calamity."
The crown prince said:
"The folly in the world,
has even greater instances.
Lǔ, inheriting the legacy of the Duke of Zhōu,
with the teachings of Confucius,
upholds benevolence and embraces virtue,
harboring no desires toward neighboring states,
yet Qí raises troops to attack it,
caring not for the people's lives,
seeking only spoils.
Qí, recklessly attacking Lǔ,
is unaware that Wú has mobilized all its men within its borders,
exhausted the treasury's wealth,
and exposed its army a thousand miles to attack it.
Wú, only knowing to cross borders and campaign against others' states,
is unaware that the King of Yuè will select death-defying warriors,
exit the mouth of the Three Rivers,
enter the area of the Five Lakes,
slaughter our state of Wú,
and destroy our Wú palace.
The peril in the world,
none surpasses this."
The King of Wú did not heed the crown prince's remonstrance,
and proceeded to attack Qí in the north.
The King of Yuè, hearing of the King of Wú's attack on Qí,
sent Fàn Lǐ and Xiè Yōng to lead troops stationed by the sea, connecting to the river,
to cut off Wú's route.
They defeated Crown Prince Yǒu at Gūxióngyí,
crossed the Jiāng and Huái, turned to raid Wú,
thus entering the state of Wú,
burned the Gūxū Terrace,
and seized its large boats.
Wú defeated the Qí army at Àilíng,
then turned its troops to approach Jìn,
disputing precedence with Duke Dìng without agreement.
A border messenger arrived,
reporting the Yuè uprising.
King Fūchāi of Wú, greatly afraid,
gathered the feudal lords and strategized:
"My route is distant,
whether to proceed without meeting or to advance,
which is advantageous?"
Wángsūn Luò said:
"Better to advance,
then grasp the authority of the feudal lords,
to achieve our aim.
I ask the king to command the soldiers,
to clarify orders,
encourage them with high ranks,
shame them with disobedience,
making each exhaust their loyalty unto death."
Fūchāi, at dusk, ordered to feed the horses and soldiers,
at midnight, commanded them to arm and don armor,
bridle horses, hold bits in mouths,
light fires at the forge,
and advance in stealth.
The Wú army, all with patterned rhinoceros hide, long shields, and Biǎnzhū swords,
marched in square formation.
The central army all wore white robes, white tassels, plain armor, and white-feathered arrows,
looking from afar like white flowers.
The king personally held a battle-axe,
bearing a banner, standing in formation.
The left army all wore red robes, red tassels, cinnabar armor, and vermilion-feathered arrows,
looking from afar like fire.
The right army all wore black robes, black chariots, black armor, and black-feathered arrows,
looking from afar like ink.
Armored troops numbered thirty-six thousand,
settling at cockcrow.
Once in formation,
they were one li from the Jìn army.
The sky still dark,
the king took up a drumstick, personally sounding the metal drums,
the three armies shouted and chanted,
to boost their morale,
the sound shaking heaven and moving earth.
The Jìn army, greatly startled,
did not emerge,
instead fortified their stronghold.
They then sent Tóng Hè to request an audience,
saying:
"The armies of two states should maintain friendly relations at the border,
with no scheduled conflict at noon.
Now, your great state oversteps to approach our humble army's fortifications,
dare we ask the reason?"
The King of Wú personally replied:
"The Son of Heaven has decreed,
the Zhōu house is humble and constrained,
the feudal lords' tributes,
do not reach the royal treasury,
unable to report to the gods and spirits above,
no one of the Jī surname is upheld in awe,
messengers are sent to inform,
officials never cease on the roads.
Initially, Zhōu relied on Jìn,
thus neglecting the barbarians.
Now Jìn rebels thus,
hence I come to you with urgency,
unwilling to yield precedence,
merely contending for strength.
I advance, not daring to withdraw,
if you, lord, do not command precedence,
we'll be laughed at by the feudal lords.
My service to you, lord, is decided today,
failure to serve you is also today.
Dare I trouble the messenger to come and go,
I personally await your command outside the fence."
As Tóng Hè was about to return,
the King of Wú stepped forward with his left foot to bid Hè farewell.
Upon reporting back,
he sat with the feudal lords and ministers before Duke Dìng of Jìn.
After conveying the message,
he informed Zhào Yāng:
"I observe the King of Wú's demeanor,
suggests great worries;
minor ones concern the death of a favored concubine or crown prince,
or else troubles in Wú,
major ones involve the Yuè people entering Wú,
preventing his return.
His mood shows deep distress,
his advance and retreat are rash and difficult,
we should not engage in battle.
My lord should grant him precedence,
not risk the state by contending for position.
But we cannot grant it outright,
must affirm good faith."
Zhào Yāng agreed,
entered to advise Duke Dìng:
"Among the Jī surname in Zhōu,
Wú is the elder and can take precedence,
to fulfill state rituals."
Duke Dìng consented,
ordered Tóng Hè to report back.
Thereupon,
the King of Wú, shamed by Jìn's righteousness,
withdrew his tent for the meeting.
The rulers and ministers of both states assembled,
the King of Wú addressed the duke first,
the Marquis of Jìn followed,
all ministers swore the covenant.
Wú, having taken precedence over Jìn, turned back,
not yet crossing Huángchí.
Yuè, hearing the King of Wú lingered long without return,
mobilized all troops to cross Zhāngshān,
cross the Three Rivers,
and intended to attack him.
Wú, fearing that Qí and Sòng might cause harm,
then ordered Wángsūn Luò to report their achievements to Zhōu,
saying:
"In the past, Chǔ failed to uphold its tribute duties,
alienating itself from fraternal states,
our former lord Hélǘ could not endure their wickedness,
girded his sword and raised his pī blade,
pursuing King Zhāo of Chǔ across the central plains.
Heaven recognized his loyalty,
and the Chǔ army suffered a great defeat.
Now Qí is no more virtuous than Chǔ,
nor does it respectfully obey the king's commands,
alienating itself from fraternal states.
Fūchāi cannot endure their wickedness,
donned armor and girded his sword,
going directly to Àilíng,
Heaven blessed Wú,
and the Qí army turned their blades and retreated.
How dare Fūchāi claim credit for himself?
It is the virtue of King Wén and King Wǔ that has protected and aided us.
At this time returning to Wú,
not waiting for the harvest season,
we followed the river, ascended the Huái, deepened the trenches and waterways,
emerged between Shāng and Lǔ,
and returned to report to the Son of Heaven's officers."
The King of Zhōu replied:
"Elder uncle, you have sent your son here,
to unite the states under one rule—this is fitting,
I truly commend it.
If the elder uncle can assist me,
then we shall together receive eternal blessings,
what worries would the Zhōu house have?"
Then he bestowed a bow and crossbow at the royal steps,
to enhance his title and posthumous name.
The King of Wú returned from Huángchí,
rested the people and disbanded the troops.
In the twentieth year, the King of Yuè raised an army to attack Wú,
Wú and Yuè battled at Zuìlǐ.
The Wú army was greatly defeated,
troops scattered,
the dead beyond counting.
Yuè pursued and crushed Wú,
the King of Wú was trapped and desperate,
sent Wángsūn Luò to kowtow and sue for peace,
as Yuè had done before.
The King of Yuè responded:
"In the past, Heaven gave Yuè to Wú,
but Wú did not accept it.
Now Heaven gives Wú to Yuè,
how can this be refused?
I request to offer the land of Gōuyǒngdōng,
and I and you shall be as two rulers!"
The King of Wú said:
"When I was in Zhōu,
I was treated with the courtesy due to a former king, given a meal.
If the King of Yuè does not forget the righteousness of the Zhōu house,
and allows me to be a dependent territory,
that would also be my wish.
The envoy requests peace in accordance with the principles of allied states,
if only Your Majesty would consider it."
Grand Master Zhǒng said:
"Wú has been unprincipled,
now we are fortunate to have captured them,
I hope the king will decide their fate."
The King of Yuè said:
"I will destroy your altars of land and grain, and level your ancestral temple."
The King of Wú fell silent.
Seven times peace was requested,
but the King of Yuè would not listen.
In the twenty-third year,
in the tenth month,
the King of Yuè again attacked Wú.
The state of Wú was exhausted and could not fight,
its soldiers scattered,
the city gates undefended,
and so Wú was slaughtered.
The King of Wú led his ministers in flight,
traveling day and night,
for three days and three nights,
until they reached Qínyúháng Mountain.
His heart filled with sorrow and worry,
his vision blurred,
his steps erratic,
his stomach empty and mouth hungry,
he picked raw rice and ate it,
bending down to drink water from the ground.
He looked to his attendants and asked:
"What is this called?"
They replied:
"This is raw rice."
The King of Wú said:
"This is what Gōngsūn Shèng predicted - being unable to eat cooked food and fleeing in panic."
Wángsūn Luò said:
"Eat your fill and let's go.
Ahead is Xū Mountain,
where we can hide in the western slope."
The king proceeded,
and after a while,
found raw melons that had ripened.
The King of Wú picked and ate them.
He asked his attendants:
"Why do melons grow in winter,
and why don't people nearby eat them?"
His attendants said:
"They're called manure-planted things,
which people don't eat."
The King of Wú asked:
"What does 'manure-planted' mean?"
His attendants said:
"In midsummer,
when people eat raw melons,
they relieve themselves by the roadside.
The seeds then grow,
but autumn frost damages them,
so people don't eat them."
The King of Wú sighed:
"These are what Wǔ Zǐxū called 'morning food'."
He said to Grand Master Pǐ:
"I executed Gōngsūn Shèng
and threw him at the peak of Xū Mountain.
I fear the shame of being condemned by the world,
my feet cannot advance,
my heart cannot go on."
Grand Master Pǐ said:
"Between death and life,
defeat and success,
can one really avoid them?"
The king said:
"True.
But does he really know nothing?
You go ahead and call him.
If Shèng is there,
he should answer immediately."
The King of Wú stopped at Qínyúháng Mountain,
calling out:
"Gōngsūn Shèng!"
Three times he called,
and Shèng answered from the mountain:
"Gōngsūn Shèng!"
Three calls, three answers.
The King of Wú looked up to heaven and cried:
"Can I ever return?
I would serve Shèng for generations."
Soon after,
the Yuè troops arrived,
surrounding Wú three times.
Fàn Lǐ stood in the central line,
holding a drum in his left hand,
and a drumstick in his right, beating it.
The King of Wú wrote on an arrow and shot it toward Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ's army,
saying:
"I've heard that when the cunning hare dies,
the good hound is cooked.
When an enemy state is destroyed,
the strategist ministers must perish.
Now Wú is suffering,
why should you ministers worry?"
Minister Zhǒng and Chancellor Lǐ urgently attacked.
Minister Zhǒng wrote on an arrow and shot back,
saying:[93"The heavens are vast and blue,
existing yet elusive.
I, your servant Zhǒng of Yuè King Gōu Jiàn, dare to say:
Previously Heaven granted Yuè to Wú,
but Wú refused to accept,
thus Heaven reversed it.
Gōu Jiàn revered Heaven and achieved merit,
and having returned to his state,
now Heaven rewards Yuè's merit,
which we reverently accept,
not daring to forget.
Moreover, Wú has six great faults,
leading to its downfall.
Does the king know them?
Having loyal minister Wǔ Zǐxū die for his honest advice,
is the first great fault.
Gōngsūn Shèng speaking directly without reward,
is the second great fault.
Grand Master Pǐ being foolish and flattering,
frivolous and slanderous,
speaking recklessly,
yet being listened to and employed,
is the third great fault.
Qí and Jìn having no rebellious conduct,
no excessive extravagance,
yet Wú attacked these two states,
humiliating their rulers and ministers,
destroying their altars of land and grain,
is the fourth great fault.
Moreover, Wú and Yuè share the same tones and musical pitches,
aligned with the stars above,
and the same principles below,
yet Wú invaded and attacked,
is the fifth great fault.
Previously Yuè personally killed Wú's former king,
a crime of the utmost gravity,
yet you fortunately attacked it,
disobeying Heaven's mandate and abandoning your enemy,
later becoming a great trouble,
is the sixth great fault.
The King of Yuè respectfully engraves this on the blue sky above,
daring not to disobey the mandate?"
Minister Zhǒng said to the King of Yuè:
"Midwinter's energy is settled,
Heaven will execute.
If we don't carry out Heaven's execution,
we'll suffer disaster instead."
The King of Yuè reverently bowed,
saying:
"Yes.
Now to deal with the King of Wú,
what should be done?"
Minister Zhǒng said:
"Wear the robe of five victories,
gird the Bùguāng sword,
hold the Qūlú spear,
glare and speak loudly to seize him."
The King of Yuè said:
"Yes."
Then according to Minister Zhǒng's words, he told the King of Wú:
"Truly, today we hear the mandate."
After a moment,
the King of Wú did not kill himself.
The King of Yuè again sent word, saying:
"How can the king endure such humiliation and thick shame!
There are no rulers who live ten thousand years in the world,
death and life are the same.
Now you still have remaining honor,
why must we have our troops raise blades against the king?"
The King of Wú still refused to kill himself.
Gōu Jiàn said to Zhǒng and Lǐ:
"Why don't you two execute him?"
Zhǒng and Lǐ said:
"We,
in our positions as ministers,
dare not execute a ruler.
We hope you will urgently command it,
Heaven's punishment should be carried out,
and cannot be long delayed."
The King of Yuè again glared angrily and said:
"Death
is what people detest.
What is detestable
is being guilty before Heaven,
and failing people.
Now you bear the crime of six faults,
yet feel no shame and desire to live,
isn't that despicable?"
The King of Wú then sighed deeply,
looked around in all directions,
and said:
"Yes!"
Then he drew his sword and fell on it, dying.
The King of Yuè said to Grand Master Pǐ:
"You, as a minister,
were disloyal and untrustworthy,
destroying the state and ruining your ruler."
Then he executed Pǐ along with his wife and children.
As the King of Wú was about to fall on his sword,
he looked to his attendants and said:
"I am ashamed in life,
and will be ashamed in death.
If the dead have consciousness,
I would be ashamed before my predecessors underground,
and cannot bear to see the loyal ministers Wǔ Zǐxū and Gōngsūn Shèng.
If they have no consciousness,
I would have failed in life.
After death, I must cover my eyes with connected silk ribbons."
Fearing it would not cover,
I wish to add another three layers of silk embroidery,
to serve as a veil for the light.
In life, do not let me be seen clearly,
in death, do not let my form be visible.
How can I bear it!"
King Yuè then buried King Wú with due rites,
at Bēiyóu on the Qínyúháng Mountain.
King Yuè ordered his soldiers to gather for the merit of our military efforts,
each contributing a handful of soil to bury him.
Zǎi Pǐ was also buried beside Bēiyóu.
The former lord of Yuè, Wúyú,
was a descendant of Xià Yǔ.
Yǔ's father, Gǔn,
was a descendant of Emperor Zhuānxū.
Gǔn married a woman from the Yǒushēn clan,
named Nǚxǐ,
who, though of mature age, had not yet borne children.
While playing at Dǐ Mountain,
she found a Job's tear and swallowed it,
feeling as if touched by someone,
and thus became pregnant,
giving birth to Gāomì through a cut in her side.
They resided in Xīqiāng,
at a place called Shíniǔ.
Shíniǔ is located in the western rivers of Shǔ.
During Emperor Yáo's time,
a great flood surged,
submerging the land,
blocking the nine provinces,
and obstructing the four waterways.
The emperor worried about the turmoil in the central realm,
grieving for the suffering of the people,
so he commanded the Four Peaks,
to recommend the virtuous and capable,
to take charge of flood control.
From the central realm to distant regions,
none recommended anyone,
and the emperor had no one to appoint.
The Four Peaks then recommended Gǔn to Yáo,
but the emperor said:
"Gǔn defies orders and ruins his clan,
he is not suitable."
The Four Peaks replied:
"Among all ministers, none compare to Gǔn."
Yáo employed him to control the floods,
but after nine years of effort,
he had not succeeded.
The emperor angrily said:
"I knew he could not do it."
He then sought another,
and found Shùn.
He had him act on behalf of the Son of Heaven,
touring the lands.
Observing that Gǔn's flood control had no visible results,
he executed Gǔn at Yǔ Mountain.
Gǔn threw himself into the water,
transforming into a yellow bear,
and became the deity of the Yǔ Abyss.
Shùn and the Four Peaks recommended Gǔn's son, Gāomì.
The Four Peaks said to Yǔ:
"Shùn, due to the failure in flood control,
recommends you to continue your father's task."
Yǔ replied:
"Yes!
I dare to fully undertake my father's work to follow heaven's will,
only to devote myself entirely!"
Yǔ grieved that his father's task was unfinished,
traveling along the rivers and upstream,
crossing all waters and surveying the Huái,
he toiled his body and worried his mind,
for seven years.
He did not listen to music,
passed by his home without entering,
ignored his hanging hat,
did not retrieve his lost shoes,
yet before success was achieved,
he sorrowfully pondered.
Then he consulted the "Yellow Emperor's Central Classic,"
a record by the sages,
which stated:
"In the southeast of the Jiǔ Mountains,
there is a celestial pillar called Wǎnwěi.
The Red Emperor resides there,
on its peak, supported by patterned jade,
covered by massive rocks,
its texts are on golden slips,
with characters of green jade,
bound with silver,
all engraved with writing."
Yǔ then traveled east and ascended Héng Mountain,
sacrificing a white horse with its blood,
but did not obtain what he sought.
Yǔ then climbed the mountain,
gazing skyward and sighing.
In a dream, he saw a man in red embroidered robes,
who called himself the Xuányí Cāngshuǐ Messenger.
"I heard the emperor sent Wénmìng here,
so I came to await him.
It is not the right time yet,
but I will inform you of the date,
do not sing or play idly,
thus I lean and sing at Fùfǔ Mountain."
Turning east, he said to Yǔ:
"If you wish to obtain my mountain god's book,
fast below the Yellow Emperor's Cliff,
on the third month, day Gēngzǐ,
climb the mountain and lift the stone,
the golden-slip text will be there."
Yǔ withdrew and fasted again.
On the third month, day Gēngzǐ,
he ascended Wǎnwěi Mountain,
uncovered the golden-slip text,
consulted the golden slips and jade characters,
and grasped the principles of water control.
Returning to the mountain,
he rode four vehicles to traverse the rivers,
starting from Huò Mountain,
circling and gathering at the Five Peaks.
As the poem says:
"Trust that southern mountain,
tamed by Yǔ alone."
He then toured the four waterways,
consulting with Yì and Kuí.
Traveling to famous mountains and great marshes,

he summoned their spirits to inquire about the veins of mountains and rivers, the locations of metals and jades, the kinds of birds, beasts, and insects, and the customs of the eight directions, the distances of different lands and foreign territories,
having Yì record them in detail.
Thus, it was named the "Classic of Mountains and Seas."
Yǔ reached thirty without marrying,
arriving at Tú Mountain,
he feared time was running out,
losing his chance,
so he declared:
"If I am to marry,
there must be a sign."
Then a nine-tailed white fox appeared before Yǔ,
Yǔ said:
"White
is the color of my garments.
The nine tails
are the proof of kingship.
The song of Tú Mountain says:
'Graceful white fox,
with nine tails lush.
Our home blessed and fine,
guests come as kings.
Establishing family and home,
I create their prosperity.'
The connection between heaven and man here
is clear and evident!"
Yǔ thus married a woman of Tú Mountain,
named Nǚjiāo,
from Xīn to Rén to Guǐ to Jiǎ days.
Yǔ traveled for ten months,
and Nǚjiāo gave birth to Qǐ.
Qǐ was born without seeing his father,
crying day and night.
As Yǔ journeyed,
he had Tàizhāng measure east and west,
and Shùhài gauge north and south,
expanding the breadth of the eight extremes,
calculating the dimensions of heaven and earth.
Yǔ crossed the river south to inspect water management,
a yellow dragon bore the boat,
frightening those aboard,
but Yǔ laughed calmly and said:
"I receive my mandate from heaven,
exerting myself to labor for the people.
Life
is nature;
death
is fate.
What are you doing?"
His expression unchanged,
he told the boatmen:
"This is heaven's means to aid me."
The dragon dragged its tail, released the boat, and left.
Heading south, he planned at Cāngwú,
and saw a bound prisoner,
Yǔ stroked his back and wept.
Yì said:
"This person committed a crime,
he deserves this,
why weep for him?"
Yǔ replied:
"When the world is orderly,
people do not suffer guilt.
When the world is chaotic,
even the good are implicated.
I hear if one man does not plow,
some will starve;
if one woman does not weave,
some will freeze.
I govern water and land for the emperor,
stabilizing the people's lives,
ensuring they have their place.
Now that they face punishment like this,
it shows my virtue is too weak to transform the people.
Hence, I weep in sorrow."
Thereupon,
he traveled throughout the realm,
east to the farthest traces,
west to Jīshí,
south beyond Chì'àn,
north past Hán Valley,
circling Kūnlún,
inspecting the six guardians,
mapping the geography,
naming metals and stones.
He charted the Liúshā in the western corner,
He channeled the Ruò Shuǐ to the northern Hàn.
Qīng Quán and Chì Yuān divided into cave openings,
connecting to the river flowing eastward to Jié Shí.
He dredged the nine rivers from hidden depths,
opened five waterways in the northeast,
excavated the Dragon Gate,
and cleared the Yī Quē pass.
Leveling the land and examining the soil,
he observed the earth and divided the provinces.
Distant regions each sent tribute,
offering their contributions,
and the people left rugged lands
to return to the central kingdom.
Yáo said:
"Yes!
Use this to secure Jì."
Then he titled Yǔ as Bó Yǔ,
appointed him as Minister of Works,
granted him the surname Sì,
and put him in charge of touring the twelve regions.
When Yáo passed away,
Yǔ observed the three-year mourning period,
as if for his own parents,
weeping by day and sobbing by night,
until his breath could no longer form sounds.
Yáo abdicated to Shùn,
who recommended Great Yǔ,
changing his office to Minister of Education,
assisting internally in the Yú position,
and externally overseeing the nine regions.
When Shùn passed away,
he abdicated and commanded Yǔ to rule,
but Yǔ mourned for three years,
his body emaciated,
his face dark and haggard.
He yielded the throne to Shāng Jūn,
retreating to the south of Yáng Shān and north of Yīn Ē.
The myriad people did not follow Shāng Jūn,
but instead sought out Yǔ's location.
They were like startled birds soaring to the sky,
or frightened fish diving into the depths,
singing by day and chanting by night,
climbing heights and calling out loudly,
saying:
"If Yǔ abandons us,
whom shall we look up to!"
After Yǔ completed the three-year mourning,
grieving for the people and having no alternative,
he ascended the Son of Heaven's throne.
After three years of evaluating achievements,
and five years of stabilizing governance,
he traveled throughout the realm,
returning to Dà Yuè,
ascending Máo Shān to receive homage from all directions,
with all ministers observing.
Among the central region lords,
Fángfēng arrived late,
and was executed as a warning to all,
showing the world all belonged to Yǔ.
He then convened a grand assembly to discuss ways of governing the state,
internally praising the cautious efforts at Fǔ Shān,
externally displaying sage virtue to match heaven's will.
Thus he renamed Máo Shān as Kuài Jī Shān.
There he transmitted state governance,
rested and nurtured the myriad people,
naming the state Xià Hòu.
He enfeoffed the meritorious,
titled the virtuous,
leaving no transgression, however small, unpunished,
and no merit, however minor, unrewarded.
The world looked up to him,
like children longing for their mother,
or sons returning to their father,
and he remained in Yuè.
Fearing his ministers might not follow,
he declared:
"I have heard that those who eat the fruit
do not harm the branch.
Those who drink from the water
do not muddy the stream.
I obtained the Fù Fǔ texts,
enabling me to eliminate the world's disasters,
returning the people to their villages,
such brilliant virtue,
how could it be forgotten?"
Thus he accepted advice and listened to remonstrance,
settled the people and built dwellings,
cleared mountains and cut timber for settlements,
carved seals,
and set horizontal beams as gates.
He standardized weights,
balanced measures,
dug wells for the people,
establishing these as standards.
Phoenixes perched in trees,
luán birds nested nearby,
qílín paced in courtyards,
and all kinds of birds dwelled in the marshes.
As he grew old with gray hair,
he sighed:
"My evening years approach,
my lifespan nears its end,
this is where it stops."
Commanding his ministers, he said:
"After my passing through generations,
bury me at Kuài Jī Shān,
with reed outer coffin and paulownia wood inner coffin.
Dig a pit seven feet deep,
not reaching the water table,
with a mound three feet high,
and three steps of earthen tiers for burial."
He added:
"Do not alter the fields, lest those dwelling find joy
while those working suffer."
After Yǔ's demise,
all auspicious signs departed.
Heaven praised Yǔ's virtue and honored his achievements,
sending the birds back to assist people in farming,
with distinctions in size,
order in movement,
cycles of prosperity and decline,
and constant comings and goings.
Upon Yǔ's death,
the throne passed to Yì.
Yì mourned for three years,
never speaking without remembering Yǔ.
After mourning ended,
Yì yielded to Yǔ's son Qǐ at the south of Jī Shān.
The lords left Yì to pay homage to Qǐ,
saying:
"Our lord
is the son of Emperor Yǔ."
Thus Qǐ ascended the Son of Heaven's throne,
ruling the state of Xià.
Following the excellence of Yǔ's tributes,
he cultivated all nine provinces' lands,
planting the five grains,
with continuous harvests year after year.
Qǐ sent envoys seasonally in spring and autumn to sacrifice to Yǔ in Yuè,
establishing an ancestral temple on the southern mountain.
Six generations after Yǔ came Emperor Shào Kāng,
who feared the discontinuation of Yǔ's sacrifices,
so he enfeoffed his lesser son in Yuè,
naming him Wú Yú.
When Yú first received the enfeoffment,
the people lived in mountains,
though benefiting from bird-tilled fields,
the tribute barely covered temple sacrifice costs.
They resumed farming along hills and plains,
or hunted birds and deer for food.
Wú Yú was simple and unadorned,
avoiding elaborate palace decorations,
living among the people,
and sacrificing at Yǔ's tomb in Kuài Jī seasonally.
After over ten generations of Wú Yú's line,
the last ruler was weak and incompetent,
unable to maintain independence,
becoming commoners among the masses,
and Yǔ's sacrifices ceased.
After more than ten years,
a person was born who could speak at birth,
his words being "bird calls",
chirping and twittering,
pointing to the sky toward Yǔ's tomb, saying:
"I am the descendant of Lord Wú Yú.
I will restore the former lord's sacrifices,
resume the worship at Yǔ's tomb,
seek blessings from heaven for the people,
to connect with the ways of spirits and gods."
The people rejoiced,
all assisting in honoring Yǔ's sacrifice,
offering tribute in all seasons,
together enfeoffing and establishing him,
to continue the line of Yuè lords,
restoring the sacrifices of Xià kings.
They stabilized the auspicious bird-tilled fields,
seeking destiny for the common people,
gradually establishing ruler-subject propriety thereafter,
naming him Wú Rén.
Rén begot Wú Zhōu,
and Zhōu devotedly guarded the state,
never failing heaven's mandate.
After Wú Zhōu's death,
some say came Fū Tán.
Fū Tán begot Yǔn Cháng,
and when Cháng ruled,
during the times of Wú kings Shòu Mèng, Zhū Fán, and Hé Lǘ,
Yuè's rise to hegemony began with Yǔn Cháng.
In the fifth year of King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè,
in the fifth month,
he, along with his ministers Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ, went to Wú to serve as vassals.
All his ministers escorted him to the banks of the Zhè Jiāng River,
where they held a farewell ceremony by the water,
with the army stationed at Gù Líng.
Minister Wén Zhǒng stepped forward to offer a blessing,
his words saying:
"May the August Heaven protect and aid,
so that what sinks now may rise later.
Calamity is the root of virtue,
and sorrow the hall of fortune.
Those who intimidate others will perish,
while those who submit will thrive.
Though our king is being led away,
he shall face no future disaster.
Ruler and subject parted in life,
move the Supreme Sovereign above.
All under heaven grieve in sorrow,
none untouched by this sadness.
I offer dried meat in tribute,
and three cups of wine we drink."
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè looked up to heaven and sighed deeply,
raised his cup with falling tears,
silent, without a word.
Zhǒng again stepped forward to bless:
"May our great king's virtue and longevity,
be boundless and without end.
Heaven and earth receive his spirit,
gods and deities lend him wings.
Our king is deeply favored,
with blessings and aid at his side.
Virtue dispels all calamities,
benefits receive his fortune.
Leaving that court of Wú behind,
he shall return to the land of Yuè.
As the cup of wine is raised high,
let us hail 'Long live the king!'"
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè said:
"I inherited the remaining virtue of the former king,
guarding the state at the border,
and was fortunate to rely on the strategies of you, my ministers,
thus preserving the former king's burial mounds.
Now I face humiliation and disgrace,
laughed at by all under heaven.
Is this my fault alone?
Or the responsibility of you, my ministers?
I do not know where the blame lies,
and wish for you all to discuss your views."
Minister Fú Tóng said:
"How base are these words!
In the past, Tāng was imprisoned at Xià Tái,
yet Yī Yǐn never left his side.
King Wén was confined in a stone chamber,
yet Tài Gōng did not abandon his state.
Rise and fall lie with Heaven,
survival or ruin depend on man.
Tāng changed his demeanor to please Jié,
King Wén submitted and won favor with Zhòu.
Xià and Yīn relied on force and abused these two sages,
yet both rulers humbled themselves to attain the Way of Heaven.
Thus King Tāng did not grieve over his hardship,
and King Wén of Zhōu did not see his困境 as a flaw."
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè said:
"In the past, Yáo appointed Shùn and Yǔ, and all under heaven was well-governed,
and even with the harm of the great flood,
it did not become a disaster for the people.
Abnormalities did not reach the common folk,
how much less so for a ruler?"
Minister Kǔ Chéng said:
"It is not as Your Majesty says.
Heaven has its chronological order,
and virtue has its thickness and thinness.
Huáng Dì did not decline,
Yáo passed on the Son of Heaven.
Among the Three Sovereigns,
ministers killed their rulers.
Among the Five Hegemons,
sons killed their fathers.
Virtue has its breadth and narrowness,
and spirit its heights and depths.
The present age is like a human market,
where goods are displayed with deceit,
and schemes are held to await the enemy.
If one unfortunately falls into distress,
one merely seeks to stretch out again.
If Your Majesty does not observe this,
but harbors joy and anger instead."
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè said:
"Those who employ others do not disgrace themselves,
while those who rely on themselves endanger their state.
You, my ministers, have all previously planned for unforeseen beginnings,
to overthrow the enemy and defeat the foe,
sitting to receive the blessings of Tài Shān.
Now I am stuck in such poverty,
yet you speak of Tāng and Wén's困境 leading inevitably to hegemony—
how do these words violate ritual and propriety?
A gentleman contends for every inch of time and discards pearls and jade,
yet now I hope only to be spared the worries of military campaigns,
but instead I am again caught in the enemy's grasp,
my body becoming a hired servant,
my wife a maid and concubine,
going away never to return,
dying a guest in the enemy state.
If my soul and spirit are aware,
I will be ashamed before my former lord.
If they are unaware,
my bones will be cast aside.
Why do your words, my ministers,
not accord with my intentions?"
Thereupon, ministers Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ said:
"We have heard the ancients say:
'If one does not dwell in obscurity,
one's will cannot be broad;
if one's form is not sorrowful,
one's thoughts cannot be far-reaching.'
Sage kings and worthy rulers
all encountered difficulties of hardship and distress,
suffered shame that seemed unforgivable,
were imprisoned in body yet honored in name,
humiliated in person yet glorious in reputation,
dwelling in lowliness without considering it vile,
residing in danger without considering it meager.
The Five Emperors, with their profound virtue, had no regret over endless distress,
yet still faced the worry of flooding.
Three times they endured the humiliation of violent hardship,
never free from the困境 of the three peaks.
They wept tears while suffering injustice,
walked and cried as they became slaves,
yet expounded the Changes and created the hexagrams,
and the Way of Heaven protected them.
When the time passed its due date,
adversity ended and prosperity came.
The feudal lords all rescued them by the king's command,
signs appeared like the red-maned horse and the black fox,
their ministers tied up their hair,
broke open the mountains and shattered the shackles,
returned to their states to cultivate virtue,
and then attacked their enemies.
They lifted and borrowed from across the seas,
as easy as turning over the back of the hand,
all under heaven honored them,
their achievements passed down for ten thousand generations.
Though Your Majesty is in hardship and distress,
we ministers will truly exhaust our strategies.
A sword that cuts bone lacks the sharpness for fine carving,
a spear that pierces iron lacks the convenience for splitting hairs,
and advisors who propose plans lack the rhetoric for sudden rise.
Now we have studied the patterns of heaven,
examined fallen records,
the two energies sprout together,
existence and ruin lie in different places.
When they rise, we are humiliated;
when we dominate, they perish.
Two states contend for the Way,
it is unknown which will succeed.
Your Majesty's danger
is a number in the Way of Heaven;
why must you injure yourself over it?
For good fortune
is the gate to misfortune;
blessing
is the root of calamity.
Though Your Majesty is now in a dangerous and difficult situation,
who knows it is not an omen of smooth passage?"
Minister Jì Niè said:
"Now our king, whose state is at Kuài Jī,
is in dire straits entering Wú,
his words sorrowful and bitter,
moving all ministers to tears.
Though there is resentment and bitterness in our hearts,
we are all deeply moved,
so why does our king use deceitful and boastful words,
employing them to deceive each other?
I truly cannot accept this."
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè said:
"I am about to leave and enter Wú,
and I entrust the state to you, my feudal lords and ministers.
I hope each of you will state your views,
and I will assign accordingly."
Minister Gāo Rú said:
"I have heard that Minister Zhǒng is loyal and good at planning,
the people admire his wisdom,
and officers are happy to be used by him.
If the state is entrusted to one person,
the way is sure to be maintained.
Why go against your heart and disobey fate by questioning the ministers?"
Minister Yè Yōng said:
"Minister Wén Zhǒng
is the state's pillar and beam,
the ruler's claws and teeth.
A fine steed cannot be matched in galloping,
the sun and moon cannot shine together;
if our king entrusts the state to Zhǒng,
then all laws and orders will surely be upheld."
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè said:
"The state
belongs to the former king;
my strength is weak, my position inferior,
Unable to uphold the altars of state,
and serve the ancestral temple.
I have heard that when a father dies, the son succeeds;
when a ruler perishes, his ministers draw close.
Now, abandoning affairs to you, the various ministers,
I go as a guest-official to Wú,
entrusting the state and its people
to you few gentlemen.
This is due to me,
yet it is also your concern.
Ruler and minister share the same path,
father and son share the same vital energy—
this is natural by innate disposition.
How can one consider those present as loyal and those departed as untrustworthy?
Why do you, the various ministers, in discussing affairs, sometimes agree and sometimes diverge,
causing my solitary heart to be unsettled?
To entrust the state to the worthy and measure achievements to accomplish success—
that is the ruler's charge.
To receive instruction, follow reason,
and not fail in one's duty—
that is the minister's responsibility.
I look to you, the various ministers, to use your abilities,
yet you speak only of offering your allegiance.
Alas!
How sorrowful!"
Jì Ní said:
"What our king has stated
is indeed the principle.
In the past, when Tāng entered Xià,
he entrusted the state to Wén Cí.
When the Western Lord went to Yīn,
he entrusted the state to one elder.
Now, you cherish Xià and intend to linger,
but your resolve lies in returning.
A wife going to the market instructs her heir to clean;
a ruler going into exile commands his ministers to guard.
The son is questioned about affairs;
the minister plans with his abilities.
Now, our king wishes to know the aspirations of the gentlemen,
each stating their sentiments,
presenting their capabilities,
and discussing what is fitting."
The King of Yuè said:
"The minister's argument is correct.
